text:
While electric vehicle adoption is soaring across the UK, public charging infrastructure is struggling to keep up.

After analysing DfT, OZEV and ONS data across all 364 UK local authorities, Hippo found:

The UK’s EV fleet grew 33 percent in a year, reaching 2.84 million vehicles by the end of 2025, but public charger numbers only grew by 22.8 percent. This mismatch has actively worsened the UK’s average EV-per-charger ratio, climbing from 30.6 to 33.1 electric vehicles per public charger.

London’s EV fleet actually grew just 20.9 percent year-on-year, the slowest of any UK region, while the South East (+53.5 percent), Wales (+42.9 percent) and the North East (+45.5 percent) all grew far faster, despite London being named the priority market for new investment.

Private EV ownership is now growing faster than company fleets nationally, up 41 percent year-on-year compared to 26 percent for company-kept vehicles, showing everyday drivers are switching to electric even quicker than businesses are.

Stockport is the most under-served hotspot for public charging in the country, with 685 EVs for every charger, even after charger numbers there grew by a third in the past year.

Cheshire West and Chester saw the sharpest infrastructure squeeze anywhere in the UK, its EVs-per-charger ratio degrading from 36 to 184 in just 12 months.

“Allego prioritising London makes sense on paper, but our data shows London’s EV growth is actually lagging behind the rest of the country, while places like Stockport and Cheshire West and Chester are seeing some of the sharpest charging squeezes anywhere in the UK” said Tom Preston, CEO of Hippo Leasing. “If new investment keeps flowing towards London by default, we risk widening the gap in exactly the places where demand for EVs, and for charging, is growing fastest.”

The worst pinch points are concentrated in heavy commercial and leasing hubs, where a massive influx of company-kept vehicles clashes with relatively small public-charging footprints.

title: Deadline approaching to oppose oil and gas rollbacks on public lands
description:
The federal government is moving to weaken protections against oil and gas pollution on America’s public lands, and the public has until August 24 to weigh in.
The other would weaken requirements aimed at reducing wasted natural gas and methane pollution.
EPA is reconsidering its 2024 standards to reduce methane pollution from oil and gas operations nationwide and has already weakened portions of those rules.
Congress also overturned EPA’s rule implementing the Waste Emissions Charge on large oil and gas methane polluters and delayed the charge itself until emissions reported in 2034.
Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, and oil and gas operations also release other pollutants that contribute to smog and threaten public health.
text:
The federal government is moving to weaken protections against oil and gas pollution on America’s public lands, and the public has until August 24 to weigh in.

In June, the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) proposed two rules rolling back safeguards adopted in 2024. One would dramatically reduce the bonds oil and gas companies must provide to help ensure wells are plugged and drilling sites restored. The other would weaken requirements aimed at reducing wasted natural gas and methane pollution.

Under current rules, the minimum bond covering a single federal oil and gas lease is $150,000, while an operator can provide a $500,000 statewide bond covering all of its federal leases in a state. The BLM proposes cutting those minimums to just $10,000 and $25,000, respectively.

These bonds help protect taxpayers if an oil and gas company walks away without properly plugging its wells and restoring the land. Even the Bureau of Land Management acknowledges that lowering the bonds could reduce companies’ incentives to properly reclaim well sites and increase risks to public lands and ecosystems.

That’s especially concerning given the nation’s legacy of abandoned wells. More than 117,000 unplugged orphaned wells have been documented across the United States, and researchers estimate that the country may have nearly 4 million abandoned oil and gas wells in all.

The administration is also proposing to weaken the Bureau of Land Management’s 2024 Waste Prevention Rule, which seeks to reduce natural gas wasted through venting, flaring and other releases on federal and tribal lands. Among other changes, companies seeking drilling permits would no longer have to submit waste minimization plans.

These proposals are part of a broader retreat from methane protections. EPA is reconsidering its 2024 standards to reduce methane pollution from oil and gas operations nationwide and has already weakened portions of those rules. Congress also overturned EPA’s rule implementing the Waste Emissions Charge on large oil and gas methane polluters and delayed the charge itself until emissions reported in 2034.

Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas, and oil and gas operations also release other pollutants that contribute to smog and threaten public health. One study in Texas’ Eagle Ford Shale found that women exposed to high levels of natural gas flaring had 50% higher odds of preterm birth than women with no exposure to flaring.

We should be requiring oil and gas companies to prevent pollution, conserve publicly owned resources and clean up after themselves, not weakening safeguards and leaving the public with the consequences.

text:
Sunrun is partnering with a distributed generation management platform to have residential and commercial solar-plus-storage systems reduce grid demand from hyperscale data centers.

This service with Voltus, ostensibly similar to a virtual power plant program, would allot “a portion” of capacity from Sunrun’s installed solar and storage project base to grid operators PJM and MISO, according to a press release. They can then tap into those distributed energy sources in response to data centers’ energy pull, and system owners would be paid for their energy exports.

“Meeting growing energy demand requires us to maximize every single electron available across the country,” said Sunrun CEO Mary Powell in a press release. “In collaboration with Voltus, we are providing critical capacity from home batteries supported by funding from hyperscalers. This is just the beginning of what distributed energy assets can achieve.”

Energy demand on the U.S. grid is increasing, and with it the cost of electricity, as the number of hyperscale data centers built across the country grows. These data centers are supporting generative AI technologies, like large language models such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT. In 2023, grid-tied data centers accounted for less than 5% of the country’s energy usage. But according to a study published by the Congressional Research Service, hyperscale data center proliferation could double or even triple that energy usage by 2028.

Voltus introduced its “Bring Your Own Capacity” program last year in response to increasing energy demand from data centers. The company hopes this service offers a fast solution to data center energy needs. And that urgency is growing. In June, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged grid operators to bring data centers online faster, and FERC members voted unanimously to support this initiative.

“[Bring Your Own Capacity] is about turning distributed resources into capacity the grid can count on, and maximizing value for the end user,” said Dana Guernsey, CEO of Voltus, in a press release. “This partnership brings together Sunrun’s residential scale with Voltus’s market-integrated flexibility platform so distributed capacity can support reliability, affordability, and growth as electricity demand increases.”

title: Report: New investments continue as policy changes slow U.S. clean energy manufacturing
description:
Convalt’s project is only the third clean energy manufacturing investment of more than $1 billion announced in the past 18 months.
Since the beginning of 2025, companies have canceled $39.6 billion in planned clean energy manufacturing investments and 53,400 announced manufacturing jobs.
Since 2000, more than 70% of announced clean energy manufacturing investment has occurred in congressional districts currently represented by Republicans, underscoring the broad economic benefits of domestic clean energy manufacturing.
The analysis tracks publicly announced investments, cancellations and manufacturing jobs across the clean energy sector using data from Atlas Public Policy’s Clean Economy Tracker.
Additional reports and analysis from the clean energy manufacturing series are available at https://www.edf.org/state-us-clean-energy.
text:
U.S. companies announced nearly $8 billion in clean energy manufacturing investments during the second quarter of 2026, showing private-sector demand remains strong even as recent federal policy changes slow the sector's growth. A new report released today by Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy, The State of Clean Energy Manufacturing in Q2 2026, finds those policy changes have contributed to nearly $40 billion in canceled investments and the cancellation of over 53,000 announced manufacturing jobs since the beginning of 2025.

Released as the nation marks the fourth anniversary of the Inflation Reduction Act, the single largest investment in climate and energy in American history, the report underscores both the law's success in attracting private investment and the threat recent policy changes pose to that momentum.

"Four years after the Inflation Reduction Act helped launch a clean energy manufacturing boom, this report shows that companies see what the Trump administration refuses to acknowledge: clean energy technologies are cost-competitive and here to stay," said Grace Hauser, Technical Analyst, Clean Power at Environmental Defense Fund. "Federal policies that provide long-term certainty can keep that momentum going, but recent policy changes are putting America's manufacturing competitiveness at risk."

In Q2, companies announced $7.9 billion in new manufacturing investments while canceling $2.9 billion in previously announced projects, resulting in $5 billion in net new investment. Solar manufacturing, transmission, and grid equipment drove the quarter's growth, led by Convalt Energy's planned $5 billion solar manufacturing campus in New Mexico, the largest clean energy manufacturing investment announced since the start of the current administration.

But large-scale investment announcements have become far less frequent. Convalt’s project is only the third clean energy manufacturing investment of more than $1 billion announced in the past 18 months. In the previous 18-month period, from July 2023 through December 2024, companies announced 24 projects exceeding $1 billion.

Among the report's key findings:

Companies announced 5,900 new manufacturing jobs in Q2 2026, while 2,800 previously announced jobs were canceled, primarily in electric vehicle, hydrogen electrolyzer and solar manufacturing.

Since the beginning of 2025, companies have canceled $39.6 billion in planned clean energy manufacturing investments and 53,400 announced manufacturing jobs.

Since 2000, companies have announced $244.8 billion in clean energy manufacturing investments and 331,900 manufacturing jobs, with more than 760 facilities operating or under construction nationwide.

Since 2000, more than 70% of announced clean energy manufacturing investment has occurred in congressional districts currently represented by Republicans, underscoring the broad economic benefits of domestic clean energy manufacturing.

The analysis tracks publicly announced investments, cancellations and manufacturing jobs across the clean energy sector using data from Atlas Public Policy’s Clean Economy Tracker. Additional reports and analysis from the clean energy manufacturing series are available at https://www.edf.org/state-us-clean-energy.

title: North American Battery Recycling Capacity Will Need to Expand | Union of Concerned Scientists
description:
Existing and planned electric vehicle battery recycling infrastructure is sufficient to handle retired lithium-ion batteries through 2030, but as more batteries reach the end of their useful lives in the coming years, continued expansion will be necessary.
That’s the finding of a recently published peer-reviewed article, “Future battery recycling in North America: Capacity expansion under shifting demand and circular strategies,” co-authored by Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) Clean Transportation Program Scientist Dr. Jessica Dunn.
According to the article, recycling capacity may need to expand substantially by 2035 depending on battery lifetimes, battery size, materials left over from battery production and other factors.
The researchers also found that cross-border movement of vehicles and batteries complicate projections and could make coordinated recycling systems across North America important for recovering critical materials from batteries.
Dr. Dunn’s previous research has shown that recycling can reduce the need for newly mined battery minerals, but strong policies are necessary to ensure that minerals are recovered at high rates and that recycling is done using low-impact processes with strong safeguards.

text:
ALBUQUERQUE, N.M.– U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) joined U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) in sending a letter to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) demanding the agency withdraw their proposal to roll back drinking water protections – which, if finalized, would remove federal public health limits on the amount of certain PFAS compounds in drinking water.

The senators emphasized in the letter to EPA administration Lee Zeldin that removing these health limits will expose Americans to unsafe levels of chemical that have been linked to kidney and testicular cancer, immune suppression problems, developmental harm, thyroid disease, pregnancy complication, and liver damage.

“Safe drinking water is not a partisan issue. Families across the country expect that when they turn on the tap, their water is safe to drink. Congress enacted the Safe Drinking Water Act to ensure EPA relies on the best available science to protect public health – not to weaken existing protections once the sciences has been established,” the senators wrote.

Despite the Trump administration’s ‘Make America Healthy Again’ agenda, if enacted, EPA’s proposal would rescind the 2024 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for PFAS and delay compliance for the PFOA and PFOS standard until 2031, putting the health of millions of Americans at risk.

“As far back as the 1950s, scientists observed that PFAS compound could accumulate in human bloodstreams. It took decades of advocacy and heroic scientific research to reach the historic moment in 2024 when EPA finally promulgated the very first national drinking water standards for PFAS compounds. We cannot afford to go backwards and make Americans’ health worse,” the senators concluded.

Heinrich has led efforts to protect New Mexicans from PFAS contamination. Most recently, Heinrich introduced legislation to support the development of next-generation, PFAS-free protective gear to better protect firefighters from the dangers of their work. In February, Heinrich announced he had successfully secured $159 million in the Fiscal Year 2026 (FY26) appropriations legislation for PFAs testing and remediation, supporting six military sites in New Mexico suspected of contamination from DOD activities.

In addition to Heinrich, the letter was signed by Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and U.S. Senators Tammy Bladwin (D-Wis.), Kristen Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Edward Markey (D-Mass.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Richard Blumental (D-Conn.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Jack Reed (D- R.I.), Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), Dick Durbim (D-Ill.), Ben Ray Lujan (D-N.M.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), and Cory Booker (D-N.J.).

Read the full text of the letter here and below:

Dear Administrator Zeldin:

We write in strong opposition to EPA’s proposal to rescind the 2024 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX, and the Hazard Index mixtures, while also delaying compliance for the PFOA and PFOS standards until 2031. These actions would reverse the first-ever national drinking water protections for six of the most dangerous and well-studied PFAS chemicals, despite overwhelming scientific evidence demonstrating that there is no safe level of exposure to many of these chemicals. Furthermore, there is a strong case to be made that this proposal contravenes the Safe Drinking Water Act’s anti-backsliding provision.

The agency’s proposal is inconsistent with both the scientific record and EPA’s own prior findings. The 2024 drinking water standards followed years of scientific review, public input, and economic analysis. EPA concluded that the standards would protect up to 105 million people from exposure to toxic PFAS in drinking water, prevent thousands of premature deaths, reduce tens of thousands of serious illnesses, and generate billions of dollars in public health benefits.

PFAS contamination is one of the most widespread public health concerns facing our nation. Nearly every American has PFAS in their blood, and millions of people continue to rely on drinking water contaminated with these persistent chemicals. Exposure to PFAS has been linked to kidney and testicular cancer, immune suppression, developmental harm, thyroid disease, pregnancy complications, and liver damage.

EPA has repeatedly stated that protecting Americans from PFAS is a top priority. Yet these proposed rollbacks move in the opposite direction. In addressing revisions to drinking water regulations, the Safe Drinking Water Act itself states that “each revision shall maintain, or provide for greater, protection of the health of persons.” Rather than strengthening protections, the proposal eliminates enforceable standards for four PFAS entirely and delays protections for the two most prevalent PFAS. Communities living with contamination should not be forced to wait additional years for clean drinking water while polluters and regulated entities receive regulatory relief.

Your agency has suggested that regulating only PFOA and PFOS is sufficient because these chemicals are often found alongside other PFAS. However, EPA’s own scientific record demonstrates otherwise. Other PFAS occur independently, contribute to cumulative health risks, and warrant their own enforceable protections. Removing standards for these contaminants will leave significant gaps in public health protections and create unnecessary uncertainty for water systems and states that have already begun compliance planning.

Moreover, many utilities and states have already invested substantial resources to comply with the 2024 standards using Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding and other federal assistance. Weakening the standards now undermines those investments, creates regulatory uncertainty, and penalizes communities that have acted responsibly to protect public health.

Safe drinking water is not a partisan issue. Families across the country expect that when they turn on the tap, their water is safe to drink. Congress enacted the Safe Drinking Water Act to ensure EPA relies on the best available science to protect public health—not to weaken existing protections once the science has been established.

We therefore urge EPA to withdraw its proposal to rescind the 2024 drinking water standards for PFHxS, PFNA, GenX, and the Hazard Index mixtures, reject the proposed delay for the PFOA and PFOS standards, and fully implement the 2024 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations as finalized.

As far back as the 1950s, scientists observed that PFAS compounds could accumulate in human bloodstreams. It took decades of advocacy and heroic scientific research to reach the historic moment in 2024 when EPA finally promulgated the very first national drinking water standards for PFAS compounds. We cannot afford to go backwards and make Americans’ health worse. Thank you for your consideration.

text:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) added certain foreign-produced power inverters to its “Covered List” July 28, restricting new covered inverter models from receiving the FCC equipment authorization generally necessary to be imported, marketed or sold in the United States.

Although the action has frequently been characterized as a ban on Chinese inverters, its actual scope is both broader and narrower. The FCC’s July 28 Public Notice and National Security Determination applies to covered power inverters produced in any foreign country, regardless of the manufacturer’s nationality. At the same time, the restriction is limited to a defined category of connected inverters and primarily affects new device models. Previously authorized models can generally continue to be imported, marketed and sold.

Still, the broader policy context is important. While the legal restriction is not limited to Chinese companies, Chinese-produced and Chinese-manufacturer inverter technology is a central target of the administration’s broader effort to reduce reliance on adversarial foreign supply chains. Chinese vendors represented nearly half of the U.S. inverter market in 2024 and 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie, making the action particularly consequential for Chinese suppliers and U.S. projects that have historically relied on them.

What the FCC Action Actually Does

Most radiofrequency-emitting devices must receive FCC authorization before they can be imported, marketed or sold in the United States. Under the Secure Networks Act, communications equipment determined by an authorized national-security body to pose an unacceptable risk can be prohibited from receiving that authorization, effectively excluding new covered equipment from the U.S. market. Though the FCC administers the Covered List of prohibited technologies, the authorized national-security body (typically an executive branch agency or interagency working group) makes the underlying national-security determination and submits it to the FCC.

The FCC’s inverter determination, alongside the advanced robotic devices determination, follows a White House-convened interagency national-security review that determined foreign-produced power inverters pose unacceptable cybersecurity and supply-chain risks to U.S. critical infrastructure. The interagency body identified two unacceptable risks:

Supply-chain vulnerabilities that could disrupt U.S. economic security, including sectors critical to national security, and

Cybersecurity risks threatening critical infrastructure and U.S. persons.

Power inverters perform an increasingly important function on the electric grid by converting electricity between direct current (DC) and alternating current (AC) for the ever-growing capacity of solar generation and battery energy storage technologies.

The determination cites Electrek analysis of Energy Information Administration (EIA) 2025 data and 2026 forecast that between Jan. 1, 2025, and Nov. 30, 2025, utility-scale solar added more than 22,237 megawatts (MWs) of capacity and battery storage added 13,357 MWs. EIA also projected another 37,157 MWs of utility-scale solar and 21,502 MWs of battery storage additions over the following 12 months–a combined approximately 58,658 MWs of additional inverter-based resources, or approximately 99% of forecasted new generation.

Modern inverters can also contain communications capabilities allowing remote control, monitoring and software updates. The FCC's National Security Determination notes that imported power inverters can therefore introduce new vulnerabilities into U.S. energy infrastructure or exacerbate existing ones given these advanced features and the integral role and scale of grid-connected inverter-based power generation.

Those trends increase the potential consequences of vulnerabilities in inverter technology. The National Security Determination warns that remote connectivity could potentially enable foreign firms to disable inverters, collect or exfiltrate data, facilitate access or surveillance by foreign government actors, or otherwise exploit equipment through cyberattacks. As more generation and storage depends on inverter-based technology, the security of those devices becomes increasingly consequential to grid reliability and national security.

However, the definition of covered equipment under the FCC order is important. The determination encompasses foreign-produced microinverters, string, central and hybrid or battery-based inverters that convert electricity between DC and AC and contain specified communications capabilities enabling remote communication, control, sensing, data collection or monitoring.

That limitation creates an important question. As Wood Mackenzie notes, it is unclear how broadly the restriction will apply, particularly to utility-scale central inverters using wired rather than wireless communications. Further FCC guidance will therefore be important in determining the restriction's ultimate reach, such as whether and under what circumstances inverters relying solely on wired communications fall outside the definition of covered equipment. Additional clarification could also help manufacturers, developers and financiers determine how the restriction applies to particular inverter configurations and whether modifications to communications functionality or existing product designs could affect a model’s authorization status.

The determination also covers qualifying equipment produced outside the United States regardless of the manufacturer's nationality, and the FCC clarifies that the newly covered equipment is identified by place of production, rather than by entity. Accordingly, the restriction is legally broader than a country-specific Chinese inverter ban. Nevertheless, its practical significance is particularly pronounced for Chinese manufacturers given their existing market share. The IEA estimates that, as of 2025, China accounted for about 80% of global inverter manufacturing capacity while Europe was second at only about 8% (with Germany and Austria leading). The administration continues to build on the broad national-security focus on reducing dependence on Chinese-controlled technologies and supply chains.

Previously Authorized Models Can Continue to Enter the Market

The most important near-term limitation is that the restriction primarily affects new device models seeking FCC authorization. Once equipment is placed on the Covered List, FCC rules prohibit it from receiving new equipment authorizations, and applicants must certify that equipment seeking authorization is not covered.

Previously authorized inverter models, however, can generally continue to be imported, marketed and sold. Industry analysts note that, as such, current models from major foreign suppliers such as Sungrow, which may account for approximately 50% of the U.S. utility-scale inverter market, are not automatically banned from the U.S. market. This should substantially reduce immediate disruption, according to Solar Power World.

Grandfathering existing models does not, however, eliminate longer-term procurement risk. Manufacturers routinely introduce new product generations, meaning the restriction could gradually reshape available equipment as existing product lines are replaced or updated.

A separate FCC waiver permits certain Class I and Class II permissive changes for covered power inverters authorized before July 28, 2026, including software and firmware updates that patch vulnerabilities or otherwise help maintain device functionality and compatibility, through at least Jan. 1, 2029.

Conditional Approval Provides a Transition Pathway for New Foreign-Produced Models

The restriction also does not categorically foreclose new foreign-produced inverter models. The FCC established a conditional approval process through which entities producing power inverters abroad can seek a determination from the Department of War (DoW) or Department of Homeland Security (DHS) that a particular inverter or class of inverters does not pose the identified unacceptable risks. If the FCC receives such a determination, it will update the Covered List accordingly.

The FCC's Annex A Conditional Approval guidance makes clear that this is a substantive national-security review. The FCC guidance requires applicants provide information concerning ownership and foreign-government influence; manufacturing locations and supply chains; component, software and intellectual-property origins; cybersecurity; and supply-chain concentration and vulnerabilities. Applicants must also provide a detailed, time-bound plan for establishing or expanding trusted U.S. manufacturing capacity.

Conditional approval therefore functions not simply as a permanent exception, but as another policy lever to facilitate domestic reshoring of production and reduce supply-chain vulnerabilities.

Implications for Renewable Energy Development and Financing

For renewable energy projects, the immediate effect is not necessarily a sudden prohibition on foreign inverters but more so a new source of technology, procurement and bankability risk.

Developers will increasingly need visibility into the specific inverter model being procured, where it is manufactured, whether it incorporates covered communications capabilities and its FCC authorization status. Supply and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) agreements may also need to address equipment substitutions, regulatory changes and replacement equipment that could face different restrictions.

These questions are particularly important for financing because inverters are critical equipment that must remain serviceable over a project’s operating life. Lenders, tax equity and tax credit investors may increasingly consider not only whether the installed model is authorized at closing, but whether compatible replacement equipment, firmware and technical support are likely to remain available. Further federal action also makes change-in-law protections and alternative sourcing strategies increasingly relevant.

At the same time, domestic manufacturing could scale significantly. According to Wood Mackenzie’s current projection, more than 100 GW AC of new U.S. photovoltaic (PV) and power-conversion-system inverter manufacturing capacity is slated to begin production before 2028. If that capacity materializes, Wood Mackenzie expects sufficient domestic alternatives to meet new U.S. demand.

The transition nevertheless remains significant. Wood Mackenzie estimates that more than 90% of roughly 200 GWAC of PV inverters delivered to U.S. commercial, industrial and utility-scale projects over the past decade were imported. Domestic equipment could initially carry a price premium because of higher parts, labor and manufacturing costs, although those costs could stabilize as production expands and competition increases.

For developers and financiers, that creates a familiar tradeoff: potentially higher near-term equipment costs in exchange for greater regulatory, cybersecurity and supply-chain certainty.

Inverters Restriction Another Step in the Broader Policy Shift to Protect Against and Divest from Adversarial Foreign Clean Energy Supply Chains

The FCC action should ultimately be viewed within a broader federal effort to reduce U.S. reliance on adversarial foreign supply chains for critical energy infrastructure. Although the inverter restriction formally reaches qualifying equipment produced in any foreign country, Chinese-produced and Chinese-manufacturer equipment remains a more specific policy concern given China’s market position and the administration’s broader focus on adversarial foreign technology and supply chains.

The action may also not be the administration’s final move involving inverters. Additional cybersecurity requirements, procurement restrictions or trade measures remain possible, including potentially another Section 232 investigation into inverter imports or related electrical equipment. The conditional approval process itself underscores the administration’s interest in using market access to encourage trusted domestic manufacturing.

The administration has also taken more significant action elsewhere in the solar supply chain. President Trump issued a determination August 6 following the Section 232 investigation into imports of polysilicon and its derivatives, finding additional measures necessary to address the national-security threat identified by the Commerce Department. The resulting framework includes a minimum import price and a 15% ad valorem tariff, while also providing a domestic manufacturing incentive program and exceptions for certain countries and existing contracts.

That determination, which will be examined in greater detail in our next post, demonstrates how the administration continues to simultaneously use national-security, trade and industrial-policy authorities to reshape renewable energy supply chains.

Taken together, these actions reinforce an increasingly clear direction. Renewable energy supply chains continue to be evaluated not simply based on price and availability, but also on cybersecurity, national security, country and component origin, supply-chain control and domestic manufacturing. For developers, investors and lenders, understanding those overlapping requirements, and appropriately allocating procurement, regulatory and change-in-law risks, will become an increasingly important component of project bankability.

Join policy and industry leaders at the Novogradac 2026 Fall Renewable Energy Tax Credits Conference, Nov. 5-6, in Washington, D.C., for critical insights and discussions on clean energy policy in the wake of the 2026 congressional midterm elections Nov. 3, as well as networking opportunities with key industry partners.

text:
The basics:

American Water, Essential Utilities cleared the federal HSR antitrust waiting period

Proposed merger would create a utility valued at about $63B

Combined company would serve 4.7M water connections in 17 states

Deal is expected to close by the end of Q1 2027

American Water Works Co. Inc. and Essential Utilities Inc. announced progress on their proposed merger Aug. 17.

The companies – headquartered in Camden and Bryn Mawr, Pa., respectively – said the waiting period under the U.S. Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976 expired at 11:59 p.m. Aug. 14.

According to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, the HSR Act requires companies to file premerger notifications with the FTC and the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division. The mandate also establishes waiting periods that must expire before mergers can move forward.

From the beginning

American Water and Essential Utilities Inc. announced their definitive merger agreement in October 2025.

The deal would create a leading regulated U.S. water and wastewater public utility with a pro forma market capitalization of approximately $40 billion and a combined enterprise value of approximately $63 billion, based on closing stock prices as of Oct. 24, 2025, according to the fall announcement.

Since then, the companies have received several regulatory approvals, including in Kentucky, Ohio and Virginia.

In American Water’s July 29 second quarter filing, President and CEO John Griffith said the company was “encouraged with the continuing progress we and Essential Utilities are making in merger integration planning and have received three state regulatory approvals for the merger so far.”

What’s to come

The deal is expected to close by the end of the first quarter of 2027, subject to customary conditions.

The joint company will serve 4.7 million combined connections across 17 states. It will boast $29.3 billion in combined water and wastewater rate base, according to a site dedicated to the merger. It will also serve more than 740,000 gas customer connections.

The joint company will operate as American Water and have its headquarters in Camden, the utilities said when the deal was announced. The website also noted that Essential’s Bryn Mawr and Pittsburgh offices will “maintain a strong operational presence long term.”

Griffith will serve as president and CEO, while Essential Chairman and CEO Christopher Franklin will serve as executive vice chair of the board of directors and as executive sponsor of the integration task force.

Continued investments

In the 2026 Q2 report, Griffith noted American Water “delivered solid results for the first half of the year.”

The company reported adjusted results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, of $1.61 per share, compared to $1.49 per share for the same quarter in 2025. Additionally, American Water reported $2.62 per share for the year-to-date period ended June 30, 2026, compared with $2.51 per share for the same period in 2025.

American Water also said during the first six months of the year, it invested $1.8 billion in infrastructure improvements and growth, including $346 million for regulated acquisitions.

In June, the parent company of New Jersey American Water completed its $315 million acquisition of systems across eight states from Nexus Regulated Utilities LLC. That included the utility systems of Montague Township.

The company plans to invest approximately $3.7 billion across its footprint in 2026, including acquisitions.

description:

text:
Data centers that power artificial intelligence models, reborn factories churning out fighter jets and drones, and growing fleets of electric vehicles all need clean power. Investors are betting on the startups generating and storing it.

This year, venture capital investment in companies tackling rising greenhouse gas emissions from the breakneck buildout of manufacturing and AI infrastructure had its strongest first half since 2022, hitting $26.1 billion, according to a new report from market intelligence firm Currence.

“This is a really big deal, and it’s been pulled by two sectors: low-carbon data centers and baseload power, (which is) anything that provides 100% low-carbon, 24/7 energy,” said Charles Bondu, Currence’s research lead.

Mega-rounds across low-carbon data center solutions, autonomous vehicles and energy drove a 55% year-over-year investment bump in the first six months of 2026. Venture capitalists are particularly interested in baseload power sources like geothermal and nuclear that satisfy data centers’ need for around-the-clock, behind-the-meter energy, Bondu said.

Booming venture capital investment in climate tech is lifting Los Angeles’ energy innovators. Among the biggest winners is El Segundo-based nuclear energy company Valar Atomics, which just topped its $340 million raise in March with a $1 billion series B round. The blockbuster funding puts the startup on the path to commercializing its next generation microreactor.

Another local player benefiting from the surge is Long Beach-based microgrid startup Critical Loop, whose $26 million series A round in April brought its total funds raised to $49 million. The company’s battery systems are a sought-after shortcut to megawatts of power for industrialists racing to build and operate energy-intensive facilities.

“There’s a lot of awareness among investors that to build anything, in modern conditions and techniques, you need the ability to get more power,” said Bala Ramamurthy, founder and chief executive of Critical Loop. “The utility is not responding fast enough in some cases, and so it needs to be augmented.”

Data centers drive the time-to-power point home, he said. Investors know hyperscalers like Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms Inc. and Oracle Corp. aren’t waiting the several years it can take to plug into a utility grid, so they’re funding the technology that gets them there faster.

Capital flows have picked up as startups on a similar timeline to Critical Loop, founded in 2023, become ready to deploy, Ramamurthy said.

“A couple of years ago, companies were building prototypes and proving things out in the space, and now people are infusing a lot of capital as these companies scale,” he said.

‘Bring your own capacity’

The U.S. is growing increasingly energy-hungry, and data centers, alongside electrification and onshoring manufacturing, are the key culprit. Sprouting up across the country despite widespread local opposition, facilities that train and run AI models consume as much electricity as 100,000 to 2 million households, the International Energy Agency estimates. Goldman Sachs’ commodities research team expects the U.S.’ data center power demand to reach 66 gigawatts in 2027, more than double the amount used last year.

Renewables and natural gas take the lead in meeting today’s demand. Balancing rapid expansion with corporate sustainability commitments, hyperscalers are signing long-term contracts with solar, wind, nuclear and geothermal providers before growing demand sends energy prices flying.

They’re also building on-site generation and using batteries to capture off-peak electricity in a move to “bring (their) own capacity,” said Shomik Dutta, co-founder and managing partner at Overture VC, an early-stage venture fund based in Santa Monica.

Overture has recently funded startups developing thermal batteries, connecting small-scale energy sources like batteries and solar panels to the grid, and using AI to speed up battery storage projects. To companies plotting major infrastructure projects, renewable and alternative energy is “much cheaper and more attractive,” compared to coal, oil and natural gas, whose prices tend to spike in times of economic and geopolitical volatility, Dutta said.

“The largest companies in the world are singularly focused on energy as the choke point for artificial general superintelligence,” he said. “You are seeing hyperscalers ask nuclear companies to name their price, so (there’s) a lot of dislocation between demand and supply creating a bizarre pricing world.”

While private markets have slowed down since interest rates began to climb in 2022, the tailwinds behind energy generation and storage have far outweighed the macro environment’s slumping effect, the investor said.

“The themes that Overture invests in – the infrastructure layer of AI, energy, robotics, compute, land, cabling, power electronics – these are areas that have most of the business world’s attention right now, and that backdraft has proven much more powerful than the cost of a higher interest rate,” Dutta said.

For firms already investing in renewable power, AI has supercharged the existing thesis: that a modernizing grid moving toward electrification would put energy startups in the spotlight. Explosive data center-driven demand came as a surprise to investors at Beverly Hills-based Angeleno Group, said Danny Jaffe, a partner at the clean energy-focused venture capital and growth equity firm.

“The thing that we completely missed at the time (of our founding in 2001) was that there was going to be this incredible onslaught of demand from AI and data centers that was going to fundamentally make every utility in the country short on energy,” he said.

Bringing on energy companies outside of the “data center world” and plugging them into it has been a key value-creation strategy for the firm, Jaffe said.

Ripple effect

Energy startups oriented around data centers and manufacturing facilities are garnering the most venture capital dollars, but investor interest reaches further. Surging industrial power needs are putting pressure on the existing grid and boosting the likes of Sawtelle-based Haven Energy, a home battery backup company. In December, Haven announced a $40 million series B raise, including a $15 million equity round, that’ll help the company ramp up deployment of its solar and home battery systems. Co-founder Vinnie Campo said new capital flows are freeing up capacity bottlenecks facing the energy sector as a whole.

“The big challenge everyone’s trying to solve for is, ‘How do you have enough energy capacity to meet this massive growing demand around energy?’” Campo said. “The platforms that have paths to deploying energy capacity quickly, that’s where the value is occurring in the industry right now.”

Aside from venture capital funding, Haven has enjoyed interest from private credit investors wading into energy, Campo said.

“There’s just a tremendous amount of investors we’ve seen coming into the space that historically probably were not looking at energy assets,” he said. “There’s a lot of capital chasing the trillion-dollar buildout of both power and compute across the country.”

Capital crowding at the top

Despite rising demand for clean energy projects across the board, much of that capital is circling the largest, most scalable opportunities. Venture capital’s climate tech deal count hit a five-year low, the Currence report showed, and the 10 biggest deals took 42% of all funding.

“Venture capital funds are being more selective in the bets that they’re making because we’re not in an area of free money, and their (limited partners) are asking for returns,” Bondu said. “They’re making fewer bets, and they’re placing them on more mature technologies that will have bigger check sizes.”

Investors are increasingly doubling down on previous investments to lead portfolio companies to as much scale in their given market niche as possible, Critical Loop’s Ramamurthy said.

“We’re seeing a lot of conviction from investors in this market. Everybody strongly believes that this is needed,” Ramamurthy said. “Investors have their pet companies that they are championing to solve some portion of this market.”

While strong investor interest in energy has in some ways been the “tide that lifts all boats,” the scale-is-king dynamic has also left a gap at the bottom, said alternative energy investor Seth Zeleznik.

Investment in infrastructure separate from major industrial projects has been crowded out, said Zeleznik, who founded CenterNode Group, the alternative energy investment arm of Century City-based merchant bank Forest Road Co., to fill that need. The firm, launched in April with up to $750 million in committed institutional capital, finances small commercial solar and battery projects that need help clearing permitting hurdles and getting off the ground.

“There’s just a focus on being able to put a lot of capital out at once,” Zeleznik said. “You have a lot of really great developers who’ve got small projects, but there’s no transmission mechanism (for them) to get money at this point.”

text:
At the peak of Japan’s bubble economy, a membership at Koganei Country Club outside Tokyo cost more than ¥400 million, roughly $2.8 million at the exchange rates of the day. Not the club. One membership. Golf memberships traded like securities in late-1980s Japan, and the Nikkei ran an index tracking their prices the same way it tracks stocks.

Then the bubble burst, and the country found out it had built golf the way it had built everything else in 1989: on the assumption that the line only goes up. The Nikkei Golf Membership Index peaked at 948.17 in 1990 and sat at 57.79 by 2002, about one-sixteenth of its high. Courses have been dying ever since. Japan had 2,154 of them left as of April 2025, a net 306 below the peak.

That collapse left a very specific kind of real estate scattered across the countryside: enormous, sunny, cleared, graded, drained, and already connected to a road. In 2015, a Kyoto electronics company looked at one of those corpses and saw a power plant that hadn’t been wired yet. And as of this spring, a wave of new Japanese restrictions on where solar can go has quietly turned that ten-year-old idea into some of the smartest land strategy in the country’s energy playbook.

Japan built more golf courses than golfers could use

Japan crossed 1,000 golf courses in the early 1970s and kept building for three more decades, peaking above 2,400. The sport was less a hobby than a business protocol, and during the bubble a club membership doubled as a speculative asset with a resale market and a price ticker.

The players went away faster than the courses did. Participation peaked around 12 million and had roughly halved by the late 2010s, before a pandemic-era wave of new and returning golfers pushed it back above 8 million, per the R&A’s 2023 participation count. The demographic math is still brutal: the bubble’s golfers came from Japan’s postwar baby boom, born 1947 to 1949, and that entire generation crossed 75 around 2025.

The asset side never recovered either. That Koganei membership was trading at about ¥60 million as of 2025, some 15% of its peak. A functioning 18-hole course sold for an average of roughly ¥810 million in 2022, per data compiled by Yanolja Research, which works out to around ¥45 million a hole. So hundreds of operators over the years have faced the same spreadsheet: keep mowing fairways forever for a shrinking, aging clientele, or find the land another job.

A fairway is a power plant that hasn’t been wired yet

In June 2015, Kyocera TCL Solar, a joint venture between Kyocera and what was then Century Tokyo Leasing, started driving racking into an abandoned course in Fushimi Ward, Kyoto City. The plan called for roughly 90,000 of Kyocera’s 270-watt modules, 23 megawatts of capacity, and an estimated 26,312 megawatt hours a year, enough for about 8,100 typical local households, per Kyocera’s announcement, with the power sold to Kansai Electric under Japan’s feed-in tariff.

Kyocera’s own case for the land was that dead courses offer “expansive land mass, high sun exposure, and a low concentration of shade trees.” Which undersells it. A golf course is engineered ground: the fairways were graded and compacted on purpose, the drainage was designed by professionals, the trees were removed from the playing lines decades ago, and there are service roads to every corner of the property.

Anyone who has followed what that prep work costs elsewhere can appreciate the head start. On a capped landfill in Houston, crews have to hold every panel down with concrete ballast because a single driven pile would breach the seal over the garbage. In Arkansas, the biggest solar project in American history is consuming more than 400,000 steel piles on raw farmland. On a dead fairway, you can drive piles all afternoon into ground somebody else already leveled.

The Kyoto plant came online in 2017 as the largest solar installation in the prefecture, and by the time its own financing partner described it in early 2018, it had grown into a 25-megawatt plant. There was a bonus layer of symmetry, too: Fushimi is the same ward where Kyocera set up its first major solar research center in the mid-1970s. Forty years of lab work, and the field test showed up next door wearing golf spikes.

Kagoshima never even got to play its course

The bigger project sat far to the southwest, on land straddling Kanoya City and Osaki Town in Kagoshima Prefecture. That site was zoned for a golf course more than 30 years earlier and then abandoned before anyone teed off, a bubble project that died as a drawing. Planning for its second life began in January 2014, after the local community itself pushed to repurpose the ground.

The announced version was 92 megawatts across 494 acres (2 million square meters), a footprint about the size of Monaco. The finished version, which began operation in May 2020, came in at 100 megawatts: 356,928 Kyocera modules, an expected 117,000 megawatt hours a year, and enough output for roughly 39,300 households by Kyocera’s estimate. Both golf-land plants finished bigger than announced, which is not a sentence anyone gets to write about construction very often.

It took real machinery to get there. Four companies, GF, Kyocera, Kyudenko and Tokyo Century, formed a dedicated operating company, the project cleared a year-long environmental impact assessment plus forestland development permission, and Tokyo Century arranged a syndicated loan with the Bank of Fukuoka and 17 regional banks. The result ranks among the largest solar plants on the island of Kyushu, sitting on ground that spent three decades as a paper golf course.

The model kept working after the internet moved on

The 2015 headlines faded, and the conversions kept going anyway. In April 2018, Kyocera TCL Solar completed a 29.2-megawatt plant in Yonago City, Tottori Prefecture, on 1.2 square kilometers of land originally designated for a golf course and other uses that never happened. 108,504 modules, an estimated 36,080 megawatt hours a year, power for about 12,000 households, all of it sold to Chugoku Electric.

Tottori was the harder test. It sits on the Japan Sea coast, with heavy snow and short winter daylight, terrain no one would call natural solar country. The company adapted the mounting design to the weather and built it anyway. A fourth site on the company’s repurposed-land list, a 27-megawatt project in Fukushima Prefecture, also sat on an abandoned course. With Yonago finished, this one joint venture counted 63 plants across Japan totaling roughly 215 megawatts since its founding in 2012, a chunk of it on land golf left behind.

Here’s the part with a twist of irony. Kyocera itself has since pulled back from making the hardware: it shut its Tianjin module factory in 2023 under pricing pressure from Chinese manufacturers, leaving a single domestic panel plant, and Nikkei reported the company had decided to retreat from the panel business. The fairway plants are on 20-year feed-in tariff contracts. They will likely outlast their builder’s panel division.

In 2026, Japan made this the only easy land left

To understand why this matters more now than it did in 2015, look at where the rest of Japan’s solar went. The feed-in tariff launched in 2012 rewarded output above all, and in a mountainous country with almost no spare flat land, cheap forested slopes got bulldozed for panels. According to economist Richard Katz, about 20% of Japan’s 9,200 utility-scale solar sites sit on formerly forested land prone to mudslides, and more than 230 accidents have occurred at such sites, one of which destroyed 120 homes.

Local governments revolted first. At least 175 cities, towns and villages passed their own ordinances restricting large-scale solar before Tokyo acted. Then the national government moved in one sustained push: a decision in October 2025 to rein in mega-solar by law, a Mega Solar Countermeasure Package adopted across ministries at the end of 2025, an amended Forest Act with tougher permits and penalties that took effect in April 2026, and a cabinet-approved bill on March 24, 2026 to tighten the Electricity Business Act on top of it.

Now hold that against the other half of Japanese policy. The 7th Strategic Energy Plan, approved in February 2025, wants solar delivering 23% to 29% of the country’s electricity by fiscal 2040, up from 9.8% in fiscal 2023. So Japan needs solar’s share of the grid to more than double, and possibly triple, while making it dramatically harder to build on forests and slopes. Every category of land that was already flattened, cleared and ruined for some other reason has become strategically precious. Golf courses are the largest single inventory of it in the country.

Nobody publishes a running national census of course-to-solar conversions, so the honest answer on the total is that documented projects span at least Kyoto, Tottori, Kagoshima, Fukushima, Hyogo and Okayama prefectures, and the closures that feed the pipeline haven’t slowed. The 306 courses already gone will have company.

The back nine pays the light bill now

The economics of the original plants are locked in for a while yet. Kyoto’s feed-in contract runs to 2037, Kagoshima’s to 2040, and the meters have been spinning through every policy fight described above, because nobody protests a solar plant on land that was scraped bare for leisure 35 years ago.

title: The 10 bestselling EVs in the U.S. so far in 2026, ranked - Quartz
description:
This ranking of the bestselling EVs in 2026 includes vehicles spanning a wide range of prices, from inexpensive smaller sedans to higher-end luxury vehicles with considerable power.
The 10 EVs below appear on U.S. News and cover the bestselling EVs so far in 2026.
Interior build quality runs fairly mediocre, though, and Tesla ’s reliance on a giant touchscreen for many tasks can frustrate users who prefer physical controls.
Despite these shortcomings and an underwhelming new base model, the Model Y remains one of the bestselling vehicles in the U.S., including among gas-powered and hybrid vehicles.
In keeping with Tesla ’s design ethos, the interior stays sparse, and the materials don’t particularly impress.
text:
For a long time, Tesla $TSLA seemed like the only real player in the electric vehicle market, and its models were everywhere. Over the past few years, other automakers have not only entered the market but thrived, and today dozens of electrics on sale deserve real consideration. Tesla ’s mass-market models remain common sights on American roads, especially near big cities or in areas with growing charging infrastructure, though they’re no longer the only EVs around, and sales of the high-profile Cybertruck have tanked, pushing it out of the top 10 despite SpaceX buying up a large chunk of production. Even so, Tesla still sits atop the overall sales charts.

The delivery numbers back that up. With plenty of manufacturers now building electric cars, SUVs, and trucks, something exists for nearly every buyer, and several models are selling in real volume. This ranking of the bestselling EVs in 2026 includes vehicles spanning a wide range of prices, from inexpensive smaller sedans to higher-end luxury vehicles with considerable power. The figures reflect the most recent sales data from the first half of 2026.

The 10 EVs below appear on U.S. News and cover the bestselling EVs so far in 2026. They span mainstream sedans, family-oriented SUVs and full-blown luxury vehicles, giving shoppers a genuine sense of how far the EV market has expanded beyond Tesla ’s early dominance. Federal EV tax credit changes have shaped much of this year’s sales picture, with several models on this list, including the Chevrolet Equinox EV, Ford $F Mustang Mach-E and Cadillac Lyriq, seeing meaningful sales declines tied at least partly to the loss of that incentive. Range and charging technology continue improving across the board, too, with multiple automakers adopting the NACS charging standard first popularized by Tesla and narrowing what was once a significant advantage for that brand alone. Together, these trends suggest a market growing more competitive by the month, even as Tesla continues holding its lead at the very top.

Credit: Tesla

The most popular EV on sale so far in 2026 is Tesla $TSLA's midsize Model Y crossover, with an estimated 163,454 units sold. It has outsold the number-two vehicle on this list by roughly 113,000 units in the first half of the year, buoyed by a 2025 refresh. The Model Y carries a U.S. News Rating of 8.5 out of 10 and starts at $39,990.

Despite that update, the underlying platform is old, though the Model Y still delivers incredible acceleration and deft handling, even if wheel and suspension options sometimes compromise ride quality despite 2025’s suspension updates. The EPA rates the longest-range Model Y at 357 miles, a distinctly respectable figure given the vehicle’s overall age.

The Model Y offers ample space for passengers in either row along with generous cargo room. A new Model Y L, which arrived this past August, adds a small third row and a larger cargo area. Interior build quality runs fairly mediocre, though, and Tesla ’s reliance on a giant touchscreen for many tasks can frustrate users who prefer physical controls. No Apple $AAPL CarPlay or Android Auto interface exists as a fallback for anyone unhappy with the native Tesla system.

Despite these shortcomings and an underwhelming new base model, the Model Y remains one of the bestselling vehicles in the U.S., including among gas-powered and hybrid vehicles. U.S. News’s Vehicle Testing Editor expects that trend to continue, since the 2026 version has only improved thanks to a midcycle refresh updating both styling and performance.

This mix of dominant sales and continued refinement gives the Model Y real standing as the clear leader among electric vehicles this year. Shoppers cross-shopping the Model Y against the new Model Y L should weigh the tradeoff between extra seating and cargo space carefully, since the third row adds bulk that may not suit every buyer’s daily driving needs.

Credit: Tesla

The Model 3 functions as Tesla $TSLA’s sedan and arguably its best overall vehicle, with an estimated 66,616 units sold. It rides lower than the Model Y, handles better,, and looks sportier, with a U.S. News Rating of 9.1 out of 10 and a starting price of $36,990. The Model 3 delivers quick acceleration and agile handling on twisty roads, though several German rivals still edge it out on outright performance. The EPA rates the Model 3 at about 363 miles of maximum range. Buyer interest has remained strong overall, though sales sit down 34.3% this year compared with 2025, according to Cox Automotive data.

The Tesla carries some notably desirable driver-assist technology. During testing, U.S. News’s Vehicle Testing Editor found the car’s Full Self Driving (Supervised) system navigated a wide variety of roads flawlessly with little input required, while noting the system isn’t fully autonomous despite its name, meaning full liability for the car’s actions still rests with the driver.

In keeping with Tesla ’s design ethos, the interior stays sparse, and the materials don’t particularly impress. Nominally a luxury car, the Model 3’s interior feels closer to a budget Volkswagen Jetta inside. Touch-based controls remain somewhat divisive, though a turn-signal stalk has replaced the steering-wheel-mounted buttons found on previous generations. Front-seat room and cargo space keep pace with the competition, though the rear seat suffers due to the sedan’s angled roofline.

This mix of strong performance and modest interior quality gives the Model 3 real standing as one of the most capable yet unpretentious EVs on the market. Shoppers drawn primarily to driving dynamics should test the Model 3 back-to-back against a comparable German sedan before deciding, since the gap in outright performance may matter more or less depending on individual priorities. This comparison matters most for buyers who value outright performance over brand loyalty alone. It also helps clarify whether the price gap between the two vehicles feels justified.

Credit: Hyundai

After the elimination of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, Hyundai dropped the price of the 2026 Ioniq 5, which now starts at $35,000, with 20,730 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.4 out of 10. The small SUV rides with genuine composure, offering excellent ride quality that stays soft in the best way. Drivers who want more performance can opt for the Ioniq 5 N, which delivers the most power and best handling in the lineup.

The Ioniq 5’s interior runs typical of many EVs, staying roomy with a flat floor and generous front seats. The interior design feels airy instead of cheap, since most touchpoints use quality materials throughout. Every trim gets dual 12.3-inch displays with wireless Apple $AAPL CarPlay and Android Auto.

Switching from a gas-powered vehicle to an EV requires some learning and adjustment, and the Ioniq 5 earns praise for making that transition considerably smoother by offering an easy, conventional experience alongside traditional Hyundai practicality, all without demanding drivers change existing habits or interfaces. U.S. News’s editor describes it as the electric SUV he most regularly suggests to prospective buyers.

This mix of familiar usability and genuine practicality gives the Ioniq 5 real standing as one of the most approachable EVs for drivers new to electric vehicles. Shoppers switching from a gas vehicle for the first time should prioritize the Ioniq 5 during test drives, since its deliberately conventional layout tends to ease the learning curve compared with more radically designed EVs. This step matters most for anyone unfamiliar with EV charging habits and day-to-day range management. It costs nothing but a test drive and can prevent buyer’s remorse down the road. This check matters most for shoppers who have never owned an electric vehicle before. It costs nothing but a bit of extra time and prevents frustration during the first few months of ownership.

Credit: Toyota

The Toyota $TM bZ received a simpler name and a refreshed look for 2026, and sales have climbed 89% this year as a result, reaching 17,553 units with a U.S. News Rating of 7.5 out of 10 and a starting price of $34,900. Intuitive tech, an enjoyable driving experience, and competitive range explain much of that jump, and a solid entry price paired with a decent feature set rounds out the appeal.

The bZ runs surprisingly spacious inside. Front- and second-row passengers get plenty of legroom, and while headroom stays generous up front, it tightens up somewhat in the back. Nice cloth and synthetic leather upholstery along with soft-touch plastic elevate the cabin, though dark, cheap-feeling plastic in other areas undercuts that impression somewhat. Overall build quality still runs quite well.

A boost in maximum range, now 314 miles, up from 252 miles in 2025, helps ease EV anxiety, as does the addition of a NACS, or Tesla $TSLA-style, charging port. Buyers should note that the base XLE trim doesn’t offer the longest range, since the bigger battery pack that delivers maximum range requires stepping up to the XLE Plus trim.

This mix of improved range and approachable pricing gives the bZ real standing as one of Toyota ’s most improved electric offerings this year. Shoppers focused on maximum range should confirm they’re looking at the XLE Plus trim specifically before finalizing a purchase, since the base XLE trim falls short of the vehicle’s full range potential. This distinction is easy to overlook during a quick showroom visit without careful attention to trim details. It also helps avoid the disappointment of expecting more range than the base trim actually delivers. This small check matters most for buyers who plan to rely on the vehicle for longer road trips. It also helps avoid a stressful moment far from a charger when the range is lower than expected. It costs nothing to double-check before signing any paperwork at the dealership.

Credit: Chevrolet

The Chevrolet Equinox EV shares its name with a gas-powered crossover, though it runs as a distinctly different, arguably better vehicle than its combustion-engine sibling, with 16,249 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.0 out of 10. Every model offers at least 307 miles of range, where many electric competitors fail to crack 300, and pricing starts just under $35,000, making it a legitimate alternative to similarly sized gas and hybrid SUVs. The Equinox EV runs about one size larger than the gas version on the outside while offering similar interior room, and it stays comfy and well equipped throughout.

The EV also runs considerably faster. Two configurations exist: a front-drive, single-motor version with 220 horsepower and 243 pound-feet of torque, and an all-wheel-drive, dual-motor version with 300 horsepower and 355 pound-feet of torque. Neither configuration delivers especially engaging handling, though both feel notably quicker off the line than the gas-powered Equinox. The affordable entry price has helped keep sales relatively strong despite the loss of federal EV tax credits, even though sales are down 41% so far this year as a result. Chevrolet also recently brought back an in-house competitor, the 2027 Bolt, though it hasn’t been in production long enough this year to crack the top 10 EV sellers list.

This mix of size, value and improved performance gives the Equinox EV real standing as one of the most practical electric SUVs currently on sale. Shoppers deciding between the front-drive and all-wheel-drive versions should think honestly about typical driving conditions, since the extra motor and power mainly benefit buyers dealing with snow, towing, or frequent highway merging. This honest assessment helps you avoid paying extra for capability you may rarely use. It also saves money by avoiding an upgrade that wouldn’t meaningfully improve daily driving anyway. This tradeoff matters most in regions with harsh winters or frequent long highway commutes.

Credit: Ford

Ford $F eliminated some of the Mustang Mach-E’s standard features for this model year, though many niceties remain, with 11,632 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 9.2 out of 10 at a starting price of $37,795. Sales are down 47% compared with the same period in 2025, suggesting some customers may have noticed the cuts.

Despite the reduced features, the Mustang Mach-E’s interior still feels quite nice, with comfortable seats and high-end materials throughout. The touch screen runs large with a crisp display, though physical climate controls would still improve the experience. Passengers in both rows stay comfortable, though space runs tight for three adults in the rear seats.

Some initially questioned whether the Mach-E SUV deserved to wear the Mustang name, but the sporty EV has proven it can uphold that legacy. Since its debut for the 2021 model year, the Mach-E’s hard-charging performance has proven itself worthy of the pony badge, according to U.S. News’s Senior Vehicle Testing Correspondent.

Buyers seem to agree. The Mustang Mach-E offers firm suspension, strong performance, and GT and Rally trims that add extra thrills for those who want them. Drivers more concerned with range can get up to 320 miles from the base model equipped with the extended-range battery.

This mix of sporty performance and continued brand credibility gives the Mustang Mach-E real standing as one of the most engaging electric SUVs available today. Shoppers who valued the previously standard features should compare current trim levels closely against last year’s lineup, since some amenities that once came included may now require an upgrade to a higher trim. This comparison often reveals exactly which features shifted and by how much across the lineup. It also helps buyers decide whether the current price still reflects fair value overall. This comparison matters most for returning owners upgrading from an earlier model year. It also helps set fair expectations before signing paperwork on a new purchase.

Credit: Rivian

The Rivian $RIVN R1S impresses through its utility and off-road performance, with 11,677 units sold, a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10, and a starting price of $76,990. It also rides with solid quality and good on-road manners. Anyone hesitant about the price should know it offers the best of both worlds, wrapped up with an exceptionally strong interior and a considerable feature set.

The R1S comes with three different power options. Two, three, or four motors and three battery pack sizes let buyers dial in what matters most to them: performance or range. The Quad-Motor version delivers a mind-boggling 1,025 horsepower rating, while the dual-motor setup with the Max battery pack achieves up to 410 miles of range.

Seating for seven people across three rows comes standard in the R1S. Though the third row runs tight, the first and second rows stay spacious throughout. The interior looks and feels distinctly luxury-grade, with roomy first- and second-row seating, according to U.S. News’s vehicle testing editor. The Rivian ’s touch-heavy controls can be polarizing, and it offers no Apple $AAPL CarPlay or Android Auto option.

This mix of rugged capability and genuine luxury touches gives the R1S real standing as one of the most versatile three-row electric SUVs on the market. Shoppers torn between motor configurations should think carefully about whether performance or range matters more day-to-day, since the Quad-Motor setup sacrifices some range for its considerable horsepower advantage. This tradeoff becomes clearer when you weigh actual daily driving habits against occasional long trips. It also helps avoid buyer’s remorse after choosing raw power over practical everyday range. This tradeoff matters most for families weighing weekend adventures against longer cross-country trips. It also helps buyers avoid overpaying for horsepower they rarely use in daily traffic. It costs nothing to think this through carefully before committing to a specific configuration.

Credit: Honda

The Honda $HMC Prologue, co-developed with General Motors $GM, stands as the first EV Honda sold in the U.S., debuting in 2024 as an initial hot seller before buyer interest cooled. Sales are down 48.5% from last year, with 8,407 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.1 out of 10 at a starting price of $47,400. Honda has since made drastic changes to its EV and hybrid plans, and it will discontinue the Prologue after this year.

The Prologue offers sleek styling firmly in the traditional Honda mold, though it’s essentially a Chevy Blazer EV underneath, distinguished mainly by Apple $AAPL CarPlay. Handling stays refined and confident, and ride quality runs well throughout. Neither the single- nor dual-motor powertrains rank as the quickest in the segment, though both handle most driving scenarios with ease. The Prologue also delivers up to 308 miles of range.

The Prologue’s interior amounts to a bit of a mixed bag. Both rows offer ample legroom and headroom, and cargo capacity stays plenty adequate. The rear seats run a touch stiff, though, and hard plastics fill much of the cabin.

Still, a U.S. News reviewer praises the Prologue’s all-day comfort up front, noting that after several hundred miles behind the wheel, the front seat remained comfortable without causing fatigue or soreness.

This mix of solid comfort and an uncertain future gives the Prologue real standing as one of this year’s more bittersweet electric SUV stories. Shoppers still interested in the Prologue despite its discontinuation should factor resale value into their decision, since discontinued models sometimes depreciate faster than vehicles with a longer expected production run. This consideration matters most for buyers planning to sell or trade in within just a few years. It also helps set realistic expectations for what the vehicle might be worth later on. This consideration matters most for buyers planning to keep the vehicle for only a few years.

Credit: Lexus

The 2026 Lexus RZ has improved range and power over previous versions, and buyers have taken notice: sales are up a remarkable 106.8% this year, reaching 7,814 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10 at a starting price of $46,000, according to Cox Automotive data. A strong feature set and good-looking styling help explain the jump, though the base RZ 350e still lacks some oomph with only 221 horsepower. Range stays merely so-so at 301 miles, and the interior doesn’t distinguish itself enough from its Toyota $TM siblings.

Even so, the interior uses premium materials throughout, and the RZ starts at a comparatively low price for its class. It runs roomy and quiet, fully earning its luxury designation. The switch to a NACS port for 2026 brings a welcome update for faster charging. Overall, the RZ delivers a great, quiet cruising experience with a comfortable ride.

Buyers hoping to upgrade to the RZ 550e F-Sport get more power and features across the board, though that upgrade comes at a higher cost, both financially and in terms of range, which tops out at only 229 miles on that particular trim.

This mix of dramatic sales growth and genuine luxury polish gives the RZ real standing as one of this year’s most improved electric SUVs. Shoppers deciding between the base RZ 350e and the upgraded 550e F-Sport should weigh the power gain against the range tradeoff honestly, since the more powerful trim sacrifices meaningful driving distance in exchange for extra thrills. This honest tradeoff helps buyers decide whether the extra power justifies the shorter driving range. It also prevents disappointment for buyers expecting the F-Sport to match the base model’s range. This tradeoff matters most for buyers who prioritize acceleration over maximum driving distance. It also helps buyers avoid disappointment if they expected the upgraded trim to match the base model’s efficiency. It costs nothing to compare both options before deciding.

Credit: Cadillac

Sales may be down 18.7% year over year, but the Cadillac Lyriq continues to impress new buyers, with 7,578 units sold and a U.S. News Rating of 8.6 out of 10 at a starting price of $59,200. It has also spawned an entire lineup of desirable EVs from the American luxury brand. As Cadillac’s first electric, the Lyriq stands as a distinctly world-class effort. Unlike many of Cadillac’s earlier comeback vehicles, it looks and feels special, with a beautifully detailed interior, and it drives exactly as a Cadillac should: quiet and relaxing when desired, but powerful and strong when pushed. That powerful side got a boost this year with the debut of the 615-horsepower, 650 pound-foot Lyriq V.

Plenty of desirable features round out the package too, from a large 33-inch dash display to a Super Cruise hands-free driving system, all at a price lower than electric alternatives from Rivian $RIVN, Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Genesis. Its considerable success has helped make Cadillac feel desirable again, boosting sales of the smaller Optiq and larger Vistiq models too. The loss of EV tax credits has hurt the Lyriq like many other vehicles on this list, though it remains a solidly strong pick overall.

This mix of luxury polish and brand momentum gives the Lyriq real standing as one of the most influential electric vehicles shaping Cadillac’s broader comeback. Shoppers comparing the Lyriq against pricier European rivals should factor in the Super Cruise hands-free driving system, since this feature often costs considerably more as an add-on elsewhere in the luxury segment. This comparison often reveals real value once you weigh the full feature set against the sticker price. It also helps buyers see past badge prestige alone when comparing similarly priced luxury EVs. This comparison often reveals real savings once you factor in every included feature. It also helps buyers feel confident they’re getting genuine value instead of paying purely for the badge.
