text:
Report Overview

In 2025, the Global String Inverter Market was valued at USD 4.9 billion, and between 2026 and 2035, this market is estimated to register a CAGR of 6.9%, reaching about USD 9.5 billion by 2035. Asia Pacific held a dominant market position, capturing more than a 47.60% share, holding USD 2.33 billion in revenue.

The string inverter industry is expanding alongside solar photovoltaic deployment, as these power electronic systems convert direct current from module strings into grid-compatible alternating current.

In April 2026, the International Energy Agency Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme reported that global photovoltaic capacity approached 3 terawatts in 2025, with about 698 gigawatts added during the year, while nearly 40 countries installed at least 1 gigawatt. This scale supports demand for efficient, managed string inverter platforms across distributed and utility installations.

Key Takeaways

The global string inverter market was valued at USD 4.9 billion in 2025.

The global market is projected to grow at a CAGR of 6.9% and is estimated to reach USD 9.5 billion by 2035.

On the basis of phase, three-phase dominated the market, constituting 79.90% of the total market share.

Based on the power rating, 41 kW to 80 kW dominated the string inverter market, with a substantial market share of around 34.50%.

Based on the end user, commercial and industrial (C&I) led the market, comprising 41.00% of the total market.

Among the connection types, on-grid held a major share in the string inverter market, accounting for 77.50% of the market share.

In 2025, Asia Pacific was the most dominant region in the string inverter market, accounting for 47.60% of the total global market.

Industrial momentum is also visible in the United States, where utility and commercial solar projects require reliable conversion, monitoring, and grid-support functions. In July 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported 2025 total solar photovoltaic capacity of 209,304.0 megawatts, including 149,798.5 megawatts at utility-scale facilities and 59,505.5 megawatts at small-scale facilities. This installed base increases opportunities for single-phase and three-phase string inverters across residential, commercial, industrial, and utility applications.

In March 2026, Eurostat reported that renewables supplied 47.3% of European Union electricity generation in 2025. Solar accounted for 27.5% of renewable electricity and recorded 24.6% growth from the previous year. Higher solar penetration increases the importance of inverter efficiency, voltage management, remote diagnostics, reactive power capability, and compatibility with storage and modern grid requirements.

Government and regulatory initiatives are also shaping technology development. In July 2025, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission approved reliability standards for inverter-based resources, requiring connected generators to ride through voltage and frequency disturbances. Separately, the U.S. Department of Energy currently lists $217 million for its Solar Energy Technologies Office Laboratory Call for fiscal years 2025 to 2027, $33 million for inverter-based resource management tools, and $26 million for solar and wind grid-services demonstrations, supporting advanced inverter research and reliable renewable integration.

Phase Analysis

Three-Phase dominates with 79.90% due to its suitability for higher-capacity commercial and utility solar systems.

In 2025, Three-Phase held a dominant market position, capturing more than a 79.90% share. Its leadership reflects strong use across commercial, industrial, and utility solar installations where higher power handling, balanced electrical loads, and efficient grid connection are important. Three-phase string inverters support larger photovoltaic arrays and can serve rooftop, carport, ground-mounted, and other distributed projects. Their scalability and compatibility with higher-capacity systems make them practical for developers seeking efficient conversion and reliable operation across demanding solar applications.

In July 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, 2025 small-scale solar photovoltaic capacity reached 40,474.8 megawatts in the residential sector, 16,031.4 megawatts in the commercial sector, and 2,999.3 megawatts in the industrial sector.

Single-Phase is the growing segment. Its adoption is supported by residential and smaller distributed solar systems where simpler electrical architecture and lower power requirements make single-phase equipment practical. These inverters provide straightforward installation, conversion, monitoring, and grid interaction for household photovoltaic systems. Continued expansion of rooftop solar and home energy systems is widening opportunities for compact string inverter solutions suited to residential electricity networks in many markets.

Power Rating Analysis

41 kW to 80 kW dominates with 34.50% due to strong suitability for commercial and industrial solar installations.

In 2025, 41 kW to 80 kW held a dominant market position, capturing more than a 34.50% share. This power band suits commercial rooftops, industrial facilities, carports, and smaller utility projects that need higher conversion capacity without moving into large centralised equipment. String inverters in this range offer scalable system design, multiple string inputs, remote monitoring, and easier maintenance, making them practical for businesses expanding photovoltaic capacity while managing installation space, operating costs, and grid connection requirements.

In June 2026, according to SolarEdge, its Synergy Power Series covered 50 kW to 120 kW, supported 175% direct current oversizing, and could deliver up to 10% more energy when paired with the company’s power optimizers.

Up to 10 kW is the growing segment. Demand is supported by residential rooftops and smaller commercial photovoltaic systems where compact equipment, straightforward installation, and lower power requirements are important. These inverters match household and light-business electricity needs while supporting monitoring and grid interaction.

End User Analysis

Commercial and Industrial (C&I) dominates with 41.00% as businesses expand solar installations to manage energy costs and consumption.

In 2025, Commercial and Industrial (C&I) held a dominant market position, capturing more than a 41.00% share. This leadership reflects strong solar adoption across factories, warehouses, offices, retail facilities, data centers, and other business sites seeking lower electricity costs and greater energy control. String inverters suit these installations because they support modular system design, multiple photovoltaic strings, remote monitoring, and easier maintenance while allowing projects to expand capacity as energy demand grows.

In July 2026, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, residential small-scale solar photovoltaic generation reached 7,212 thousand megawatthours in May 2026, while year-to-date generation totaled 28,405 thousand megawatthours and rolling 12-month generation reached 66,319 thousand megawatthours.

Residential is the growing segment. Demand is supported by expanding rooftop solar adoption, household electrification, energy storage integration, and interest in reducing grid electricity purchases. Residential string inverters provide compact power conversion, monitoring, safety functions, and compatibility with home photovoltaic arrays. Their modular design also supports different roof layouts and system sizes, making them suitable for homeowners seeking flexible solar installations and improved control over household energy production across diverse markets.

Connection Type Analysis

On-Grid dominates with 77.50% as grid-connected solar remains the preferred setup across major installations.

In 2025, On-Grid held a dominant market position, capturing more than a 77.50% share. Its leadership reflects the widespread use of grid-connected solar systems across residential, commercial, industrial, and utility installations. On-grid string inverters convert photovoltaic output for direct use and grid export while supporting monitoring, voltage control, and system protection. Their compatibility with established electricity networks and net-metering frameworks makes them practical for projects seeking reliable solar integration without depending entirely on standalone storage.

In April 2026, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency, off-grid electricity capacity outside Eurasia, Europe, and North America expanded by 1.7 gigawatts during 2025, with solar power contributing 1.5 gigawatts of that increase.

Off-Grid is the growing segment. Demand is supported by remote communities, telecom sites, farms, islands, and other locations where grid access is limited or unreliable. Off-grid string inverters can operate with photovoltaic arrays, batteries, and backup generation to provide independent electricity supply. Continued deployment of decentralized renewable systems is widening opportunities for inverter solutions that support energy access, resilience, and flexible power management in areas beyond conventional grid infrastructure worldwide today.

Driver Analysis

PV Capacity Build-out and Inverter Content Demand

Solar deployment remains the primary volume engine for string inverters because every new PV installation requires power-conversion equipment, while distributed and segmented utility-scale plant layouts raise inverter-unit intensity relative to large centralized designs. Global solar PV additions reached roughly 602 GW in 2024, with utility-scale capacity accounting for approximately 382 GW and rooftop/distributed systems adding about 200 GW; cumulative global PV capacity reached around 2.25 TW by year-end.

China added about 315 GW of solar capacity in 2025, lifting its installed PV base to about 1.2 TW, while the national 2026 solar outlook remains substantial at an estimated 180–240 GW despite a post-policy-change normalization in installation momentum. In the United States, developers plan 43.4 GW of utility-scale solar additions in 2026 51% of planned new utility-scale generation capacity creating direct demand for high-power three-phase string inverters, monitoring gateways, skid integration, and long-term service agreements.

Drivers Impact Analysis

Restraint Analysis

Grid Interconnection Delays

Grid congestion is the most material near-to-medium-term restraint because string inverter demand is ultimately recognized at system commissioning, not when a PV project enters development, secures land, or places a preliminary equipment order. The International Energy Agency has identified at least 3,000 GW of renewable projects waiting for grid connection globally, including around 1,500 GW in advanced stages, a backlog equivalent to roughly five times the solar-and-wind capacity added in 2022.

Europe faces similar friction, with grid-connection queues documented in at least 16 countries and approximately 120 GW of mature renewable projects plus 1.5 million household installations potentially lacking timely grid access by 2030. For inverter vendors, delayed energization extends receivables cycles, increases inventory-aging risk, weakens factory-load visibility, and lowers service-attachment conversion because EPCs defer procurement until connection certainty improves; the estimated -1.8 percentage-point CAGR drag reflects delayed revenue recognition rather than permanent destruction of every underlying PV opportunity.

Restraint Impact Analysis

Opportunity Analysis

Storage-Ready Hybrid Platforms

Hybrid PV-storage products represent an upside opportunity rather than a baseline string-inverter driver because a large share of installed solar capacity still operates as a grid-export-only asset, while integrated storage, bidirectional conversion, backup operation, load optimization, and virtual-power-plant participation remain underpenetrated across residential, C&I, and smaller utility applications. Global battery-storage deployment reached 108 GW in 2025, up 40% year-on-year, with installed capacity approximately 11 times its 2021 level; about 80% of new capacity was utility-scale, leaving the remaining behind-the-meter segment as a relatively less-developed inverter-led value pool.

A manufacturer that converts a conventional 10–30 kW commercial string-inverter sale into a hybrid package can expand system revenue through battery interface hardware, energy-management software, ATS/backup equipment, monitoring, commissioning, and service coverage; a modeled hybrid configuration can generate 1.5–2.5 times the inverter hardware revenue of a basic grid-tied unit while lifting gross-margin potential by roughly 5–10 percentage points where software and service are attached.

The estimated +1.9 percentage-point CAGR upside is most achievable in the United States, Europe, Australia, India, and MENA, where demand charges, time-of-use tariffs, grid outages, curtailment risk, and peak-shaving economics can justify the additional capital cost, provided manufacturers secure battery OEM interoperability, bankable warranties, installer training, and financing partnerships before hybrid architecture becomes a commoditized standard.

Opportunity Impact Analysis

Challenges Analysis

Distributed Fleet O&M

Distributed string-inverter architectures improve redundancy but create an operational scaling problem because a 100 MW plant using 250 kW string inverters may require approximately 400 inverter assets, versus one or a small number of central conversion systems, each with separate communication addresses, cooling systems, connectors, firmware versions, alarms, and potential service events. This does not stop current deployments, but it raises lifetime operating complexity in harsh environments and can erode the levelized-cost advantage of distributed designs if fleet management is weak.

A field-service model that requires even one technician visit per 100 inverter-years can translate into four annual interventions for a 100 MW distributed fleet before accounting for communication faults, fan maintenance, pest damage, dust ingress, connector degradation, and firmware remediation; in MENA, India, Latin America, and Australia, travel distance and harsh operating conditions can raise the cost of each truck roll by 30–60% relative to dense urban C&I service areas.

The modeled -0.8 percentage-point CAGR friction arises from higher warranty provisioning, spare-parts buffers, training requirements, and customer skepticism about long-term serviceability; mitigation depends on predictive analytics, standardized field-replaceable units, regional spares hubs, digital work orders, remote commissioning, and O&M contracts priced on availability rather than reactive repair.

Challenges Impact Analysis

Geopolitical Impact Analysis

Geopolitical Realignment and Trade Restrictions Reshaping String Inverter Supply Chains

Geopolitical tensions are reshaping the String Inverter Market through trade barriers, semiconductor exposure, supply chain concentration, and localization policies. The U.S. Department of Energy states that 80% to 100% of manufacturing capacity across each solar supply chain step is located in China or Southeast Asia. Disruptions can delay solar projects and inverter procurement.

Trade measures are increasing cost uncertainty. The Office of the United States Trade Representative raised Section 301 tariffs on Chinese solar wafers and polysilicon to 50%, effective January 1, 2025, while semiconductor tariffs increased to 50% in 2025. Because string inverters rely on power semiconductors, these measures can influence sourcing, economics, and supplier diversification.

In April 2025, the U.S. Department of Commerce issued final antidumping and countervailing duty determinations on solar cells from Cambodia, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam. Final dumping margins included 125.37% for Cambodian exporters and 111.45% for Trina Solar Thailand, increasing uncertainty for developers sourcing equipment from Southeast Asia.

In Europe, industrial policy is encouraging regional manufacturing. The European Commission reported in 2026 that the Net-Zero Industry Act targets domestic manufacturing capacity equal to up to 40% of annual deployment needs by 2030, while €445 million had supported solar manufacturing. These measures encourage localization, but inverter suppliers remain exposed to semiconductor availability, tariff changes, and sourcing shifts.

Regional Analysis

Asia Pacific dominates with 47.60% and USD 2.33 billion, while North America is the fastest-growing region.

In 2025, Asia Pacific held a dominant position in the String Inverter Market, capturing more than a 47.60% share and generating USD 2.33 billion. The region benefits from large-scale solar deployment, expanding distributed photovoltaic systems, and demand from commercial, industrial, and utility projects.

In February 2026, China’s National Energy Administration reported that photovoltaic capacity reached 1.2 billion kilowatts, including 670 million kilowatts of centralized solar and 530 million kilowatts of distributed solar, supporting inverter demand across the region.

North America is the fastest growing region, supported by utility-scale solar expansion, distributed generation, grid modernization, and rising demand for power conversion. In February 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported that developers planned 86 gigawatts of new utility-scale generating capacity for 2026, with solar representing 51% of planned additions. This strong project pipeline creates favorable conditions for string inverter suppliers serving commercial, industrial, residential, and utility-scale solar installations across the region.

String inverter manufacturers focus on grid-forming capability, power-density improvement, digital monitoring, and storage compatibility to strengthen competitiveness. SMA Solar Technology also broadened its portfolio, unveiling three-phase hybrid inverters from 5 kVA to 30 kVA with storage capacities from 3.2 kWh to 49 kWh for homes and small businesses.

Competition is increasingly shaped by product range, system integration, service reach, and software-led performance. Sungrow continues to offer string inverters spanning 2 kW to 352 kW across residential, commercial, and large-scale applications. SolarEdge expanded its MultiRange concept across its European commercial photovoltaic inverter portfolio in June 2026, while SMA reported a €1.41 billion order backlog at the end of March 2026. The system was introduced for residential applications in locations with unstable or limited grid access, expanding GoodWe’s off-grid solar and storage portfolio.

title: Centrus Energy to make thousands of centrifuges in Oak Ridge | Exclusive
description:
Centrus Energy already has a customer - with a presence in Oak Ridge - that is expecting to buy its special uranium fuel by the end of the decade.
Centrus Energy has a 16-centrifuge demonstration cascade that is producing a small amount of HALEU in Piketon.
“This large-scale manufacturing effort at the Oak Ridge facility is designed to support the entire next-generation advanced reactor market, commercial utilities and national security needs,” Jordan said.

text:
The Centrus Energy Corp. plant located at the end of Centrifuge Way in Oak Ridge is gearing up to accelerate its construction of 45-foot-tall AC100M centrifuge machines in the next three years, according to Ben Jordan, a local spokesman for the company.

Centrus Energy already has a customer - with a presence in Oak Ridge - that is expecting to buy its special uranium fuel by the end of the decade.

In response to a question, he added that the Oak Ridge plant will be producing “thousands of uranium enrichment centrifuges for use by Centrus Energy’s American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio.”

The additional centrifuges, he stated, are needed to enable the Piketon facility to produce enough High Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) – nuclear fuel for advanced reactors in which the uranium is enriched in fissionable uranium-235 at a level of 19.75% – to meet customer demands by 2029. Centrus Energy has a 16-centrifuge demonstration cascade that is producing a small amount of HALEU in Piketon.

“This large-scale manufacturing effort at the Oak Ridge facility is designed to support the entire next-generation advanced reactor market, commercial utilities and national security needs,” Jordan said. “This multi-billion-dollar scaling effort is backed by the recent $900 million Department of Energy task order.”

A high-profile customer for Centrus Energy HALEU is Oklo Inc., which like Centrus Energy has a presence in Oak Ridge.

In June, Oklo and Centrus Energy announced a partnership in which the latter will supply a large amount of HALEU to Oklo by 2029 for Oklo’s fast-fission reactors that will be built in Ohio to power Meta’s data centers used to train artificial intelligence models.

Under the Letter of Intent, Centrus will supply enough HALEU from Piketon to power, for many years, five of Oklo’s Aurora powerhouses, which are electricity-generating fast reactors. This fuel will support Oklo’s planned 1.2-gigawatt Clean Energy Campus in southern Ohio, which is backed by tech giant Meta to power its AI data centers.

Centrus expects its first new large-scale enrichment capacity to come online in Piketon in 2029, the exact year deliveries to Oklo are scheduled to begin, Jordan said.

On Sept. 4, 2025, Oklo Inc. announced plans to invest up to $1.68 billion to develop the nation’s first privately funded, commercial-scale, advanced nuclear fuel recycling facility on a 248-acre parcel it purchased in Heritage Center Industrial Park in west Oak Ridge. The Advanced Fuel Recycling Center, which will offer 800 permanent jobs, will likely produce new nuclear fuel in the 2030s from used nuclear fuel it will accept from the Tennessee Valley Authority’s seven reactors in its three nuclear power plants.

In the 2030s, after the Oklo fuel recycling plant is operational, some Oklo fast reactors will begin burning new nuclear fuel produced in Oak Ridge from used fuel.

Nuclear companies in or associated with Oak Ridge plan to build high-temperature, advanced reactors that will need HALEU in coated uranium particles embedded in graphite-covered, golf-ball-size TRISO fuel. The reactor companies are Kairos Power, Radiant Nuclear and X-energy, which is building the TRISO-X fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge.

For future advanced reactors in the nation, Centrus is expected to be the most important source of HALEU fuel by the end of the decade, and BWXT (with a presence in Oak Ridge) will potentially be a leading fabricator and supplier of HALEU-TRISO fuel.

Centrus has begun manufacturing centrifuges to support its uranium enrichment expansion at its centrifuge manufacturing factory in Oak Ridge by relying upon a domestic manufacturing supply chain. Centrus started expanding its manufacturing capacity in Oak Ridge in late 2024 and announced the expansion in January. Centrus has already begun hiring in Tennessee and Ohio to support the project.

Centrus Energy already has a customer - with a presence in Oak Ridge - that is expecting to buy its special uranium fuel by the end of the decade.

In response to a question, he added that the Oak Ridge plant will be producing “thousands of uranium enrichment centrifuges for use by Centrus Energy’s American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio.”

The additional centrifuges, he stated, are needed to enable the Piketon facility to produce enough High Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) – nuclear fuel for advanced reactors in which the uranium is enriched in fissionable uranium-235 at a level of 19.75% – to meet customer demands by 2029. Centrus Energy has a 16-centrifuge demonstration cascade that is producing a small amount of HALEU in Piketon.

“This large-scale manufacturing effort at the Oak Ridge facility is designed to support the entire next-generation advanced reactor market, commercial utilities and national security needs,” Jordan said. “This multi-billion-dollar scaling effort is backed by the recent $900 million Department of Energy task order.”

A high-profile customer for Centrus Energy HALEU is Oklo Inc., which like Centrus Energy has a presence in Oak Ridge.

In June, Oklo and Centrus Energy announced a partnership in which the latter will supply a large amount of HALEU to Oklo by 2029 for Oklo’s fast-fission reactors that will be built in Ohio to power Meta’s data centers used to train artificial intelligence models.

Under the Letter of Intent, Centrus will supply enough HALEU from Piketon to power, for many years, five of Oklo’s Aurora powerhouses, which are electricity-generating fast reactors. This fuel will support Oklo’s planned 1.2-gigawatt Clean Energy Campus in southern Ohio, which is backed by tech giant Meta to power its AI data centers.

Centrus expects its first new large-scale enrichment capacity to come online in Piketon in 2029, the exact year deliveries to Oklo are scheduled to begin, Jordan said.

On Sept. 4, 2025, Oklo Inc. announced plans to invest up to $1.68 billion to develop the nation’s first privately funded, commercial-scale, advanced nuclear fuel recycling facility on a 248-acre parcel it purchased in Heritage Center Industrial Park in west Oak Ridge. The Advanced Fuel Recycling Center, which will offer 800 permanent jobs, will likely produce new nuclear fuel in the 2030s from used nuclear fuel it will accept from the Tennessee Valley Authority’s seven reactors in its three nuclear power plants.

In the 2030s, after the Oklo fuel recycling plant is operational, some Oklo fast reactors will begin burning new nuclear fuel produced in Oak Ridge from used fuel.

Nuclear companies in or associated with Oak Ridge plan to build high-temperature, advanced reactors that will need HALEU in coated uranium particles embedded in graphite-covered, golf-ball-size TRISO fuel. The reactor companies are Kairos Power, Radiant Nuclear and X-energy, which is building the TRISO-X fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge.

For future advanced reactors in the nation, Centrus is expected to be the most important source of HALEU fuel by the end of the decade, and BWXT (with a presence in Oak Ridge) will potentially be a leading fabricator and supplier of HALEU-TRISO fuel.

Centrus has begun manufacturing centrifuges to support its uranium enrichment expansion at its centrifuge manufacturing factory in Oak Ridge by relying upon a domestic manufacturing supply chain. Centrus started expanding its manufacturing capacity in Oak Ridge in late 2024 and announced the expansion in January. Centrus has already begun hiring in Tennessee and Ohio to support the project.

name: Texas Environment
title: Data Centers and Historic Heat Test Texas' Business Strategy - Bloomberg Law
description:
Houston once set out to build “the world’s most air-conditioned city,” which is fine until the power grid fails.
Now the grid has a new power drain that can run around the clock: data centers training and operating artificial intelligence systems.
The goal is to ensure that large users only connect in quantities and locations the Texas grid can reliably support.
AI data centers add a different kind of load: large, concentrated, and continuous.
The Texas Business Court offers a specialized forum.
text:
Texas has spent two legislative sessions making itself the premiere state for incorporation. Whether it’s a state you can actually operate in is a different question, and the answer looks less certain in August than it did in May.

In recent weeks, the “feels like” temperature across the Houston metro area climbed above 100 degrees. Houston once set out to build “the world’s most air-conditioned city,” which is fine until the power grid fails. Air conditioning isn’t comfort here; in prolonged heat, it’s public-safety infrastructure.

Texas asks more of that infrastructure every day. The state added 391,243 residents between July 2024 and July 2025, reaching 31.7 million — about 2.6 million more people than in 2020. Population growth means more homes, offices, hospitals, and air conditioners. Now the grid has a new power drain that can run around the clock: data centers training and operating artificial intelligence systems.

Texas is unusual in a structural sense, too. Unlike the rest of the Lower 48, Texas runs on its own grid, which the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, known as ERCOT, operates. ERCOT mostly escapes Federal Energy Regulatory Commission jurisdiction because it doesn’t cross state lines.

That independence became a liability in February 2021, when Winter Storm Uri forced the largest controlled outages in US history. Since then, the Legislature, the Public Utility Commission of Texas — which regulates ERCOT — and generators have mandated weatherization, restructured ERCOT’s board, and adopted reliability standards meant to keep a statewide failure from happening again.

That’s why the Texas Senate Business & Commerce Committee’s July 29 hearing focused on electric reliability, including Senate Bill 6. SB 6, the large-electric-load law effective June 20, 2025, standardizes ERCOT interconnection for data centers and other power-intensive users, makes them share infrastructure costs, and allows curtailment during grid emergencies.

ERCOT reached an unofficial all-time July peak of 91,089 megawatts on July 22, breaking a record set the day before, Chair Charles Schwertner said in the hearing. The grid still held more than 20,000 megawatts in reserve, without a conservation call or emergency. That’s reassuring. It isn’t permission to stop planning.

Possible projects totaling 474 gigawatts — more than five times that July peak — are in the pipeline. ERCOT therefore created “Batch Zero,” which studies large users together and screens for financial security, site control, equipment orders, and whether the grid can reliably serve them.

The goal is to ensure that large users only connect in quantities and locations the Texas grid can reliably support. The task is no longer to attract investment; it is to distinguish an executable project from a placeholder before Texans pay to build around it.

The heat makes that challenge tangible. No single sweltering week proves climate change, but infrastructure is designed for patterns, not anecdotes. More days are expected to reach or exceed 100 degrees. Hotter days and nights extend cooling demand. AI data centers add a different kind of load: large, concentrated, and continuous. Both trends increase the cost of planning.

Gov. Greg Abbott’s (R) recent actions acknowledge the growing pressures on the grid. In June, he directed the PUC and ERCOT to prevent data centers from shifting their infrastructure costs to residential ratepayers and promised legislation addressing data centers’ added generation, water-efficient cooling, usage reporting, community impacts, and tax incentives.

Abbott on Aug. 3 ordered a comprehensive audit of data center projects seeking ERCOT interconnection and paused approvals until the review is complete. That isn’t Texas abandoning AI; it’s Texas recognizing that “business friendly” can’t mean an unlimited claim on shared power and water.

The legal framework still matters. The Texas Business Court offers a specialized forum. Senate Bill 29 supplies a management-protective governance framework. The Texas Stock Exchange moved from promise to operation when live trading began July 10, and its guide anticipates a first corporate listing in October.

These institutions lower the legal and financial cost of choosing Texas, but none of them keeps a plant running in August. Electricity, water, transmission, housing, and transportation determine whether a company can actually operate after it arrives.

This is where the usual Delaware comparison falls short. Delaware’s advantage is principally institutional: statute, court, and precedent. But incorporation reaches only internal affairs; most of what constrains how a company operates is where it does business. Incorporating in Texas doesn’t require that the company operate there, but many of the largest companies to lay down corporate stakes in the state, such as Tesla Inc. and ExxonMobil Holdings Inc., are also headquartered there.

The recent legislative changes let Texas compete on the institutional ground Delaware owns, without giving up its historic industrial capabilities. Houston’s ship channel, energy complex, highways, medical center, and embrace of air conditioning all reflect the same instinct: Law can invite growth, but infrastructure makes growth possible.

The Senate’s broader interim agenda follows that tradition. The Legislature this session says it will focus on areas essential to the external affairs of corporations, including broadband, nuclear energy, transmission, cybersecurity, and the state’s new AI law.

For boards and counsel, domicile advice shouldn’t stop with fiduciary standards and litigation exposure. The real question isn’t only which law governs the board, but which jurisdictions govern the success of the enterprise.

A Texas on-the-ground strategy requires asking when a project can interconnect, who funds transmission, whether load can be curtailed, how cooling affects local water, and whether nearby communities accept the bargain. Those are also governance questions: They determine whether management can execute the plan the board approved.

The harder question for Texas is whether it can build quickly, fairly, and with enough foresight to sustain business growth in a hotter, more power-hungry future. The July 29 hearing and Abbott’s willingness to slow the data-center pipeline suggest the state understands the challenge.

Charters are the easy part. Power, water, and transmission are the test.

Columnist Carliss Chatman is a professor at SMU Dedman School of Law. She writes on corporate governance, contract law, race, and economic justice for Bloomberg Law’s Good Counsel column.

title: How New Mexico, the Saudi Arabia of Wind, is Beating Dirty Electricity
description:
The Public Service Company of New Mexico, or PNM, said it delivered 80% carbon-free electricity in 2025 after investing in solar energy, batteries, and wind.
In the evening, solar energy stored in batteries keeps the lights on, while the wind turns turbines that meet other electricity needs.
It contains a series of renewable energy mandates, beginning with a statewide standard of 50% renewable energy by 2030.

This plant closed in 2022, and PNM opted to replace all of its capacity from the coal power plant with renewables.
text:
Although it’s part of an industry famous for changing slowly, New Mexico’s largest utility has moved quickly to update its electricity supply to cleaner alternatives.

The Public Service Company of New Mexico, or PNM, said it delivered 80% carbon-free electricity in 2025 after investing in solar energy, batteries, and wind. During the daytime, the sun powers fans, air conditioners, and more across the state. In the evening, solar energy stored in batteries keeps the lights on, while the wind turns turbines that meet other electricity needs. (For details, see part one of this story.)

This remarkable transformation to a climate-friendly system has unfolded in just five years. As recently as 2021, power plants fueled by climate-warming coal and gas generated nearly 80% of PNM’s total electricity.

“We know it’s the right thing,” said Laurie Williams, PNM’s senior vice president of integrated planning and transmission development.

An ambitious policy

Much of this progress stems from a state law passed in 2019 called the Energy Transition Act. It contains a series of renewable energy mandates, beginning with a statewide standard of 50% renewable energy by 2030. Investor-owned utilities like PMN must generate 80% of their electricity from renewable sources by 2040 and achieve 100% zero-carbon electricity by 2045.

PNM is ahead of schedule. The company said that it will meet the zero-carbon requirement by 2040, five years before the deadline.

Williams explained that the transformation of the company’s energy supply is not solely motivated by complying with state laws.

“I would say it’s been more driven by the culture,” she said.

Over her 34 years with the company, “We’ve understood more and more about climate and the impacts on climate of traditional fossil fuels,” she said. “We’ve got to be part of solving the problem,” she added. “So I think there’s been a shift in mindset.”

PNM formerly owned the majority of a large coal power plant called the San Juan Generating Station. This plant closed in 2022, and PNM opted to replace all of its capacity from the coal power plant with renewables.

‘A chance to diversify the economy here’

The Energy Transition Act sets aside money to help workers who lost their jobs due to the closure of the coal plant and nearby coal mine as well as for the development of new renewable energy in the same county as the former coal plant.

Advocates criticized the program for a three-year delay in distributing the money, but funding did get allocated and spent. The state government reported that 2,800 workers have been retrained so far, well above the target of 2,000 workers.

“There’s not a lot of opportunity in New Mexico. It’s an area that, you know, we struggle,” Williams said.

She pointed out that the state’s economy is largely dependent on oil and gas. But New Mexico’s vast renewable energy resources offer new pathways to prosperity.

“It feels like there is a chance to diversify the economy here in a way that could be really meaningful for the citizens and for the future of the state,” she said.

Many Native Americans worked at the San Juan coal plant and mine. The Energy Transition Act established a fund specifically to help Native American communities with the energy transition. Every tribe that lives near a fossil fuel power plant that closes gets automatic membership on a committee that helps decide how and where funds should be allocated.

Money has been spent on sustainable agriculture, food sovereignty, irrigation, new solar projects, worker retraining, and direct payments to displaced workers.

Small-scale solar

Utilities aren’t the only ones on a building spree. Small-scale solar installations in New Mexico more than doubled from 2020 through 2025, and PMN reports that over 13,000 of its customers have solar panels.

Those who can’t or don’t want to put solar panels on their homes can purchase small shares of large solar farms. Sixteen community solar projects operate in the state, and 31 more are planned for a total of 200 megawatts of shared solar power coming online.

The Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act granted New Mexico $156 million to help build solar power for low-income communities, but the Trump administration clawed the money back.

Not just clean, but also cheap

As New Mexico’s grid gets cleaner, the state is also avoiding the price hikes that have become common around the country.

Nationwide, residential electricity prices have spiked by 32% in the last five years (May 2021 through May 2026). In New Mexico, prices have increased by just 7% during that same time frame.

The state’s electricity prices remain below average, with residential electricity at $0.14 per kilowatt-hour in May 2026 compared to the national average of $0.18 per kWh, and household electricity bills in New Mexico are among the lowest in the country.

Photo by Jeffrey Keenan on Unsplash

One last piece of the puzzle: interconnection

When more renewables are added to a grid, more pieces need to be connected. In many locations, new renewables projects face a multiyear waiting time to be plugged into the grid, which slows the transition to cleaner energy sources.

“The moral of the renewables story is transmission,” Williams said. “You must have significant levels of interconnection to all of your neighboring entities.”

New Mexico developed policies to bring renewables online quickly, reliably, and cheaply, including quick turnaround times for reviewing and approving applications for new projects, low fees for interconnecting, and transparency in data sharing and reporting to the public. New Mexico was the only state to earn an “A” grade for interconnection policies in a recent report by the Interstate Renewable Energy Council and Vote Solar.

Williams explained some of the myriad engineering challenges that go into converting a traditional fossil-fueled electricity system into the grid of the future.

“This really is the biggest math problem on the planet to solve, kind of a generational challenge, but really, really fun and really interesting, but not at all straightforward,” she said.

A lot goes on behind the scenes every time an air conditioner kicks into gear. But at least in some places, the web of decisions, policies, and infrastructure is producing a more climate-friendly way to keep lights, fans, and air conditioners running, even in the heat of summer. And that’s pretty cool.

title: Florida residents stopped trusting the grid and started building their own "safety nets" before ...
description:
With total U.S. electricity demand projected to rise rapidly over the coming decade, that deficit becomes increasingly dangerous.
Now, a quiet shift across Florida homes and businesses is unfolding—one that centralized utility planners are failing to predict.
Natural gas fueled roughly 75% of state electricity generation in 2024, creating extreme exposure whenever supply chains face storm disruptions or price shocks.
Driven by data centers, industrial expansion, and electrification, U.S. power demand is projected to climb 21% by 2030 and 39% by 2035.
Why Florida residents feel grid stress more than most No state relies on its residential sector like Florida.
text:
Florida stands as America’s second-largest producer of electricity, yet it cannot power itself independently. The state routinely draws power from neighboring regional grids to cover the gap. With total U.S. electricity demand projected to rise rapidly over the coming decade, that deficit becomes increasingly dangerous.

This tension peaks every year between June and November, when hurricane season transforms widespread blackouts from a statistical risk into an annual certainty. Now, a quiet shift across Florida homes and businesses is unfolding—one that centralized utility planners are failing to predict.

A grid under pressure from two directions

Florida’s energy infrastructure conceals significant vulnerability. Natural gas fueled roughly 75% of state electricity generation in 2024, creating extreme exposure whenever supply chains face storm disruptions or price shocks.

Across Florida, electrical contractors report multi-year growth in pre-storm infrastructure spending by property owners unwilling to rely on utility promises.

This localized risk aligns with a broader national crunch. Driven by data centers, industrial expansion, and electrification, U.S. power demand is projected to climb 21% by 2030 and 39% by 2035. Nationally, operators hold just 26 gigawatts of reserve capacity above reliability requirements—a thin 3% buffer that is continually narrowing.

While planners focus heavily on new gas plants, utility solar, and transmission lines, they overlook a critical dynamic unfolding directly on the customer side of the meter.

Why Florida residents feel grid stress more than most

No state relies on its residential sector like Florida. Households consume 54% of all electricity used statewide—the highest share in the nation. Nearly every home runs air conditioning, and 90% rely on electric heating.

Consequently, power failures trigger immediate public safety crises. When severe storms destroy distribution lines, outages instantly threaten food supplies, medical equipment, and essential climate control.

With Florida experiencing more hurricane landfalls than any other state, prolonged blackouts are an expected annual reality. Living through them shifts how residents view public utilities, prompting proactive investment.

Solar is rising, but so is the demand it must meet

The generation mix is evolving. Wind and utility solar produced a record 17% of U.S. electricity in 2025, reaching 19% with small-scale solar included. Florida ranked third nationally in solar generation, behind only California and Texas.

However, power consumption is expanding in parallel. Population growth, expanding digital infrastructure, and electrified systems continuously absorb new generation as fast as it comes online.

Thus, utility solar expansion alone cannot eliminate operational risk. Reliability margins remain tight, leaving the central grid vulnerable.

Property-level resilience: The demand signal planners are missing

Standard forecasting models miss crucial bottom-up decisions. Across Florida, electrical contractors report multi-year growth in pre-storm infrastructure spending by property owners unwilling to rely on utility promises.

EV charger installations have similarly grown, reflecting a broader mindset shift: consumers are actively moving from hoping the grid holds to preparing for when it fails.

Because utility forecasts prioritize centralized plant construction, this uncaptured demand growth creates an expanding blind spot for grid operators.

What Florida’s pattern means for grid planning everywhere

Florida offers a vital case study for storm-exposed regions nationwide. Property-level resilience decisions draw from the same tight capacity margin as utility demand. Planners who fail to track these signals will miscalculate baseline grid requirements.

text:
North Carolina's fast-growing data center industry is meeting stronger neighborhood-level resistance as more residents say they do not want such projects close to home during the AI-driven expansion.

Here's what to know

According to NC Newsline, a statewide survey conducted at the end of July found that 53% of North Carolinians opposed data centers in their communities.

Another 20% supported them, while 27% said they were unsure.

That was a clear change from Elon University's March poll, which found 44% opposed, 24% supportive, and 32% undecided.

Opposition spanned multiple voter groups. Jason Husser, director of the Elon Poll, said the survey showed majorities of Democrats, independents, and women against local data centers, along with pluralities of Republicans and men.

The industry's support numbers fell despite a pro-data-center lobbying group spending $367,272 on a North Carolina advertising campaign focused on the business and economic upsides of data centers.

Husser said the issue carries extra weight because it is unfolding close to where people live.

"It's not just a debate in Raleigh that can be far away for people," he said. "It's a debate in their local county seats."

More background

The poll comes as communities across North Carolina grapple with what large data center projects could mean for land use, power demand, water consumption, noise, and local budgets.

More than 20 local governments in North Carolina have put moratoriums in place on new data center development, while they evaluate the issue and decide which rules should apply to future proposals.

At the same time, some local officials have pushed back against moratoriums, arguing that data centers could generate valuable property tax revenue. The debate has become increasingly visible at county meetings and in city halls across the state.

Data centers support cloud computing, online services, and AI tools that can help optimize electricity systems, improve renewable energy forecasting, and boost efficiency. But they can also consume enormous amounts of electricity and water, strain local infrastructure, raise concerns about pollution and higher utility costs, and fuel broader worries about security, misuse, and unintended social consequences as AI expands.

What's being done?

Many communities appear to be trying to slow the process rather than stop it outright.

Moratoriums can give local governments time to study likely impacts, hear from residents, and write zoning or permitting rules that fit local infrastructure and development goals.

Husser told NC Newsline he was not surprised that the advertising push has struggled to win people over, especially when residents are focused on how projects could affect their own neighborhoods.

Public hearings, planning board meetings, and county commissioner sessions can shape whether projects move forward, what restrictions apply, and how benefits and burdens are distributed.

In cases like this, local rules around water use, energy demand, buffering, and tax agreements can directly affect everyday life.

As Husser put it, "We've seen in the past that grassroots NIMBY movements can move the needle more than significant corporate spending, particularly when people are skeptical of those corporations to begin with."

name: Clean Energy
title: After a 2-year wait, will Ohio's largest solar project get the OK? - Canary Media
description:
The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County and three of its townships.
Oak Run Solar would bring 800 megawatts of solar and 300 MW of energy storage to a state that has become increasingly hostile to clean energy, even as mounting electricity demand increases power prices and threatens grid reliability.
The OPSB’s staff has already weighed in: Its Aug. 7 brief asks the full board to confirm Oak Run’s permit.
“The project represents a significant opportunity for long-term economic investment in Madison County while supporting Ohio’s growing energy needs,” Samantha Sawmiller, senior development manager for the Oak Run Solar Project, told Canary Media.
The Ohio Supreme Court’s multiple opinions on May 26 in the Oak Run case may also suggest a growing partisanship among some of its members.
text:
Following a key legal deadline last Friday, the stage is now set for the Ohio Power Siting Board to make a final decision about whether the state’s largest solar and energy storage project to date can move ahead.

The OPSB initially approved the Oak Run Solar Project in March 2024, but the case has since been bogged down by an appeal filed by Madison County and three of its townships.

Oak Run Solar would bring 800 megawatts of solar and 300 MW of energy storage to a state that has become increasingly hostile to clean energy, even as mounting electricity demand increases power prices and threatens grid reliability.

Though the county and townships filed their appeal with the Ohio Supreme Court in October 2024, it was not until this past May that the court weighed in. A majority of the seven justices rejected all objections to the project except one.

To deal with that issue, the court sent the case back to the board with instructions for regulators to ​“more thoroughly address the Oak Run project’s visual impacts,” specifically by reviewing photo simulations or artist’s sketches of how the project’s proposed substations would look from public vantage points.

On July 28, Ohio regulators heard testimony on this narrow issue. Briefing wrapped up last Friday.

Once the full board reviews the transcript, briefs, and other filings, it will issue a decision. The OPSB’s staff has already weighed in: Its Aug. 7 brief asks the full board to confirm Oak Run’s permit.

The board is under no obligation to vote according to its staff’s recommendation, and there is no specific deadline for it to act. Any additional appeal could also eat up more time.

“The project represents a significant opportunity for long-term economic investment in Madison County while supporting Ohio’s growing energy needs,” Samantha Sawmiller, senior development manager for the Oak Run Solar Project, told Canary Media. ​“We respectfully await the Ohio Power Siting Board’s decision.”

Oak Run’s saga demonstrates the difficulty of developing clean energy in Ohio. In recent years, the state has blocked 5.3 gigawatts of wind and solar projects and garnered a reputation as the place ​“where wind and solar projects go to die.”

Since 2021, the General Assembly has enacted multiple laws that create extra hurdles for new solar and wind, but not for fossil fuel projects.

Meanwhile, the OPSB has played a central role in restricting solar’s growth, especially for grandfathered projects exempted from local government bans under those state statutes.

In March, the OPSB denied permits for the proposed 94-MW Crossroads Solar Grazing Center in central Ohio. Last month, it asked the state Supreme Court to dismiss an appeal from the developer of the planned 175-MW Kingwood Solar installation, whose permits the regulators denied in 2022. The project’s interconnection agreement has expired while it awaits a court decision — a fact the board used to justify its request for dismissal.

The Ohio Supreme Court’s multiple opinions on May 26 in the Oak Run case may also suggest a growing partisanship among some of its members. Previously, the court’s members had generally shown more deference toward the OPSB’s expertise on its factual findings.

When those opinions are pieced together, six of the court’s seven justices found fault with the OPSB’s grant of the permit because the developer’s visual evidence didn’t include renderings of the project’s three substations.

Three of those justices found that was the only shortcoming. Three others also sided with the local governments and would have required more evidence on issues dealing with water, wildlife, and fears about the safety of battery storage.

Jennifer Brunner, the court’s only Democrat, would have affirmed the OPSB’s decision in its entirety, based on the case record’s other evidence.

Taken together, the opinions ​“added more confusion to an already uncertain legal environment” for utility-scale renewables, said Karin Nordstrom, a lawyer with the Ohio Environmental Council, which is a party in the case supporting the project.

“Ohio is facing a massive energy crunch and ever-rising energy prices [and] really needs a clear substantive standard for reviewing these proposed projects,” she added. ​“And that’s not what we got from the court in this case.”

Testimony at the July 28 hearing was relatively brief. Lauren Devine, director of permitting and environmental matters for Savion, the project developer, said the company had the consulting firm EDR do additional work to show how public vantage points would look with the planned substations.

Gordon Perkins, a division manager with EDR, reported on that new work and its photo simulations with the substations included. The substations ​“would not contribute to visual impacts that were not already identified” in the group’s earlier review of the Oak Run project, he said, adding that the developer would take various steps to minimize visual impacts.

Mark Bellamy, a utilities specialist on the technical staff that advises the OPSB, reported that he had reviewed the consultant’s new report and concluded that Oak Run’s aesthetic appearance would be consistent with that of other solar farms — hence the staff recommendation to greenlight the project.

The local governments’ sole witness was Errol Gattis, a resident of London, Ohio, who said he’d be able to see the project from his yard and porch and objected to EDR’s choice of vantage points.

Ohio’s rules don’t require consideration of a project’s expected appearance from every possible angle, however. And state law doesn’t guarantee that viewsheds won’t change, said Tom Bullock, executive director for the Citizens Utility Board of Ohio, a consumer watchdog group that promotes clean energy and is not part of the case.

An Aug. 7 brief filed by the opponents’ lawyer, Jack Van Kley — a longtime renewable-energy opponent in the state — took issue with the vantage points for the visual analysis and argued that the developer should have provided the materials as a supplement to the company’s project application, complete with various steps for public participation.

Those stances are similar to arguments that the Ohio Supreme Court rejected in its Oak Run ruling in May, about the general approach for a visual analysis and whether regulators had properly found that the developer’s application was complete. Moreover, the court didn’t order a supplement to the application, just the review of additional material on a single issue.

“This was the evidentiary hearing that is very narrowly focused on the simulations for the substations,” said Christine Pirik, a lawyer for the developer, when Van Kley tried to use the argument to block admission of the additional evidence into the case record.

Administrative Law Judges David Hicks and Isabel Marcelletti sided with the developer and the siting board’s staff, noting their belief that the hearing process complies with the court’s directive.

Filings by the OPSB’s staff and the Ohio Environmental Council, which advocates for clean energy, also took issue with Van Kley’s arguments. ​“The Local Governments’ alleged procedural violations apply to service requirements for an application, not supplemental evidence submitted on remand,” lawyers Karin Nordstrom and Chris Tavenor wrote in the council’s Aug. 14 reply brief.

The clock is ticking for Oak Run, as lawyers for the developer noted in a May 18 court filing: ​“Oak Run is now in dire need to have the appeals process come to a close as soon as possible.”

“Should the Project fail due to the lengthy time for considerations, Oak Run will lose its significant financial investment and the community and state of Ohio will lose the employment and financial benefits that would result from construction and operation of the Project,” including about $250 million for local governments, its filing said.

title: Hochul wants to build more nuclear power than the U.S. has in 30 years - Times Union
description:
Kathy Hochul is pushing New York headlong into building more nuclear power capacity in the coming years than the entire country has added over the last three decades.
​Most of the country’s nuclear plants — which make up roughly 20% of U.S. electricity generation — were built between the 1970s and 1990s.
The last two nuclear reactors built in the U.S. — both at the same site in Georgia — were collectively $17 billion over budget and years late.
“I’m not anti-nuclear, and I’m not advocating shutting down existing operating nuclear plants,” said Allison Macfarlane, who chaired the Nuclear Regulatory Commission from 2012 to 2014.
Hochul already tasked the New York Power Authority, a state-run entity that owns and operates power plants, to develop at least one gigawatt of the new nuclear reactors.
text:
ALBANY — Gov. Kathy Hochul is pushing New York headlong into building more nuclear power capacity in the coming years than the entire country has added over the last three decades.

At a time when lawmakers and governors across the political spectrum are increasingly open to boosting nuclear energy supply, but not crafting solid plans, she’s set a firm target to add 5 gigawatts of new energy production — enough electricity to supply nearly 4 million homes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The hope is that a bounty of reliable power would spur economic development, stabilize soaring utility bills and propel New York into an era with plentiful clean electricity. Augmenting the state’s nuclear fleet would add roughly $50 billion in benefits to the electric grid by 2050, according to the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority.

But the vision could sputter under the technology’s immense costs and protracted regulatory timeline. A spate of new reactors could require $15 billion to $24 billion in public subsidies, a state analysis found. That analysis doesn’t include additional payments residents may have to make if projects go over budget. The first new nuclear facility may not be complete until 2039, meaning it will do little to address present affordability and electric grid reliability challenges.

The initiative by New York comes as a bevy of federal tax credits and low-cost loans have been rolled out in recent years to bring new reactors online affordably and meet rising power demand, including from AI-driven data centers.

​Even with renewed enthusiasm, it’s been a challenge to get nuclear plants under construction.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“We’re in the middle of an often proclaimed renaissance in nuclear power,” said David Victor, a University of California San Diego professor who researches reducing the electric grid’s reliance on fossil fuels. “We have a lot of talk about building new reactors — and not a lot of doing.”

The next two decades may determine whether Hochul’s push is justified or whether nuclear power remains mired in controversy and cost overruns that have historically hindered the industry’s growth. Despite some of the concerns that have heightened the stigma surrounding the industry, including safe storage of radioactive waste, nuclear plants can produce enormous amounts of steady power for decades and with no greenhouse gas emissions. They also operate around the clock, unlike wind and solar projects.

​Most of the country’s nuclear plants — which make up roughly 20% of U.S. electricity generation — were built between the 1970s and 1990s. A powerful antinuclear movement grew during that period and gained momentum after incidents that included the meltdown at the Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania. Public backlash was so strong on Long Island that a nuclear facility completed there in 1984 never operated commercially.

The last two nuclear reactors built in the U.S. — both at the same site in Georgia — were collectively $17 billion over budget and years late. Last year, voters ousted incumbents from the Georgia Public Service Commission after they had hiked utility rates to pay for the new facilities.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

‘The objective at hand’

Some energy sector experts and environmentalists question the focus on building new nuclear plants when solar and wind farms are cheaper and take less time to build.

“I’m not anti-nuclear, and I’m not advocating shutting down existing operating nuclear plants,” said Allison Macfarlane, who chaired the Nuclear Regulatory Commission from 2012 to 2014. “I’m just practical. And if you’re talking about spending public money, you shouldn’t be talking about wasting public money when there’s an easier available alternative.”

But Hochul’s vision for the state’s energy system is one of abundance, where nuclear plants complement a swath of new wind and solar farms to meet New York’s ambitious mandate to utilize 100% clean energy by 2040.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nuclear is one of the only energy sources that can operate nonstop while producing no greenhouse gas emissions — which are linked to both warming the planet and negative public health outcomes. In 2024 alone, the emissions avoided by operating the four existing reactors upstate were equivalent to removing 3.5 million cars from the road, according to Brattle, an energy research firm.

Indian Point, a Westchester County plant, provided New York City with around 25% of its electricity needs until a public pressure campaign eventually led to its closure in 2021. The use of fossil fuels to offset that loss has increased, and more than 85 percent of electricity being supplied to New York City and Long Island is from gas and oil.

Every gigawatt of nuclear power — enough energy to supply 750,000 homes — can, in some cases, provide the same benefit to the grid as three gigawatts of wind, solar and battery storage, according to the Energy Research and Development Authority.

“Anyone that’s out there pushing for one specific technology, whether it be just nuclear or just renewables, isn’t necessarily serious about achieving the objective at hand,” said Richard Barlette, director of state government affairs at Constellation Energy, which operates all of New York’s nuclear plants. “Because at the end of the day, the (state’s climate) goals are so lofty you need every clean resource at your disposal.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Hochul is only looking to build new reactors in communities that want them, making Constellation a likely partner. Both Wayne and Oswego counties — where the existing nuclear plants are — have expressed interest in getting new facilities.

Building additional reactors at existing locations takes advantage of “low-hanging fruit,” because necessary heavy rail lines and water access are already onsite, Barlette said. Constellation also has already secured a grant to study putting a new reactor at one of the plants in Oswego County.

How to pay for it

Even with willing developers and communities, building new nuclear facilities is fraught with pitfalls — especially for a governor so committed to affordability, a tension Hochul has acknowledged.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“I look at projects like the very expensive nuclear project they did in Georgia,” Hochul said. “I’m working hard to make sure that we don’t get sucked up into those high costs.”

No matter how efficiently New York gets nuclear off the ground, residents will likely be on the hook for billions in subsidies to keep the plants commercially viable. The state’s current fleet of nuclear and renewable energy producers already receive subsidies, and they amount to roughly 10% of the typical residential utility bill.

What remains to be seen is how innovative state and energy sector leaders can be in bringing down the cost of new nuclear so those future subsidies are as minimal as possible.

President Donald J. Trump has ratcheted up financial programs for nuclear developers, and the Inflation Reduction Act signed by President Joe Biden in 2022 created significant tax credits for nuclear projects.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

How to cover the remaining billions that the federal government won’t guarantee is where development can get expensive for New Yorkers.

To make financing a new nuclear facility feasible, taxpayers may have to pay some added costs if a project comes in over budget, according to a report by the state Energy Research and Development Authority and Public Service Commission report.

“If you’re thinking about building a big new reactor in New York, you’re not just looking at (whether) people (are) saying nice things about your project right now,” said Victor, the University of California professor who is also on the advisory council of the Institute for Nuclear Plant Operations. “It’s, will those nice things hold when the project has cost overruns, which seems likely.”

Barlette, the Constellation Energy official, wouldn’t say whether state taxpayers would have to cover potential construction overruns for the company to invest in new nuclear projects. Holtec, a major nuclear developer, said in filings submitted to the Public Service Commission that state taxpayers could bear additional costs in the event construction goes over budget.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Where does this public support come from? It comes from the people,” said Assemblywoman Jo Anne Simon, a Brooklyn Democrat who opposes Hochul’s plan. “You spread that out across all the ratepayers, and everybody’s going to get a very significant hike.” Simon is sponsoring legislation that would institute a moratorium on public subsidies for new nuclear plants.

The state can also take some amount of ownership in new plants or provide grants to lower their costs, the Energy Research and Development Authority report stated. Hochul already tasked the New York Power Authority, a state-run entity that owns and operates power plants, to develop at least one gigawatt of the new nuclear reactors.

Hochul has suggested power-intensive businesses, like Micron’s chip fab complex near Syracuse, could receive electricity in exchange for covering some of the costs.

A spokesman for Micron wouldn’t say whether the company is interested in such an agreement but noted the company is generally supportive of the governor’s nuclear energy targets.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The most commercially viable reactor is the design constructed in Georgia. Each can consistently power 750,000 homes. Smaller designs are entering the market now but are extremely expensive and less tested.

​States are hoping that as more nuclear plants are built, both the nascent small reactors and established large-scale designs can become less expensive.

​The next generation of large reactors could be roughly 40% cheaper than the Georgia plants if a robust workforce is in place and the companies developing the projects are on firm financial footing, a 2024 Massachusetts Institute of Technology study estimated. Hochul has already dedicated $40 million to enlisting a workforce for the next generation of reactors.

But the history of nuclear development in the U.S. doesn’t show a steady decline in costs for new reactors. Throughout the 1950s and early 1960s, plants became progressively cheaper, according to a study from researchers at the Breakthrough Institute, an environmental research center. Since the late 1960s, costs for new facilities have largely escalated.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

None of the four reactors built in the U.S. over the last 30 years were on time or on budget.

‘Looking out for your safety’

​A core component of how expensive new facilities will be is how quickly they can get built. Projects have to be under construction by 2033 to fully take advantage of Biden-era tax credits. But that timeline is tighter than it looks because the federal approval process can take roughly six years.

​Hochul has encouraged the Trump administration to speed up the regulatory process. But the push puts her in a potentially vexing situation as some former regulators have raised concerns that changes under consideration by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission undermine safety.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Nuclear plants have limits on how much radiation an employee or member of the public can be exposed to every year. ​In July, the nuclear commission proposed rules eliminating a requirement that nuclear facilities keep radiation exposure to employees far below those top annual limits.

Workers at nuclear plants received an average of roughly 3% of their annual radiological exposure limit in 2024, according to commission data.

Part of the reason plants keep exposure levels so low is because of the standard the commission is seeking to remove, said Edwin Lyman, the director of nuclear power safety with the Union of Concerned Scientists.

If New York is going to provide subsidies to new reactors, they should “be put toward making the plants safer, instead of allowing the industry to cut costs,” he added.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

David Brenner, a radiation expert from Columbia University, said the proposed changes are “not unreasonable” because the commission already has rules setting the maximum amount of radiation an employee or member of the public can safely receive.

“Radiation does get a rather bad rap,” Brenner said. “The very word radiation makes people nervous.”

But the world is full of radiation, including from medical devices like X-ray machines and natural sources like fruit. It’s estimated that living near a nuclear power plant for a year exposes a person to roughly the same amount of radiation as eating a banana.

Hochul said that new nuclear reactors will be built with “safety at the forefront” and under “rigorous environmental standards.” Hochul’s administration is still reviewing the commission’s proposal, a spokesman said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

‘Has got people excited’

The nuclear industry has long been plagued with concerns over safety.

​But in the upstate communities where plants have been in operation for more than 50 years, the technology is widely popular. About 60% of Oswego County residents support building new nuclear reactors while 12% are opposed, a survey from Jefferson Community College found. Communities in that region are used to running annual safety drills and have thousands of employees working at the existing plants on a temporary or permanent basis.

​Local officials are hoping the power from new facilities will support economic development nearby.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Newsletter

Sign up here

​Hochul, when discussing the challenges of keeping New Yorkers employed and fostering economic development, often references the closure of manufacturing plants in western New York that took place during her childhood. Adding nuclear energy is about spurring an “upstate ecosystem surrounding innovation,” she said. Large businesses like Micron and GlobalFoundries already have plans to build massive facilities upstate.

​“There’s been over the last few decades some loss of manufacturing,” said Philip Church, the Oswego County administrator. “But nuclear and its employment has been steady, and so it’s a major player in our economy, a major employer. The prospect of having additional one or two plants here has got people excited.”

​Building new reactors in willing communities reduces the risk of catastrophic public backlash like what happened with the plant on Long Island or Indian Point. But Hochul’s vision is a colossal test of whether New Yorkers can reap the benefits of nuclear energy without suffering from significant overruns at a time when affordability is everything.

text:
The steel structures market in China is estimated at 100 million tonnes

In 2026, China’s steel structures sector is expected to see steady growth in demand, which remains one of the key pillars of domestic steel consumption, with an annual volume of around 100 million tonnes. However, the market is undergoing a clear structural shift: away from traditional civil engineering towards the new energy sector, high-tech manufacturing and infrastructure. This is reported by BigMint.

Sheet and processed sheet steel account for 60–70% of the total volume of steel used in steel structures. Due to the ongoing contraction in the residential construction sector, the main drivers of growth are renewable energy projects, industrial facilities, data centres and transport infrastructure.

Key areas of consumption:

Industrial construction and IT. Thanks to the development of industrial parks, cold-storage logistics centres and data centres, the use of all-steel frames – which ensure rapid assembly – is expanding.

Energy infrastructure. This sector is expected to become the strongest driver of growth. The production of solar mounting systems, wind turbines and substations is significantly increasing demand for hot-rolled and galvanised coils, as well as heavy plate.

Transport and urban infrastructure. The construction of bridges, railway stations and sports facilities ensures stable consumption of heavy sections and pipes, although this depends on funding schedules.

At the same time, the qualitative structure of consumption is changing: the share of high-strength steel grades (above Q355), weather-resistant and corrosion-resistant alloys is growing. In the long term, China’s decarbonisation policy and the development of prefabricated construction will contribute to a further increase in the share of steel structures in the country’s total crude steel consumption.

title: Old buildings, new standards: How cities can upgrade existing housing | SCEWC 3
description:
The majority of the homes that will exist in most cities in 2050 have already been built.
Rehabilitating them —improving energy performance, accessibility, structural safety, and housing quality— is one of the most pressing and complex challenges of urban housing policy.
At the same time, ageing housing stock is both a social challenge and a climate opportunity, especially when inefficient or inaccessible buildings are occupied by lower-income or elderly households with limited capacity to invest in improvements.
The session will address how cities can scale renovation and retrofit through coordinated action between governments, building owners, residents, finance institutions, and the construction sector, ensuring that upgrades improve affordability, quality of life, and neighbourhood resilience.

text:
The 40-year-old remains of a dry cleaning company are pushing UNC student Emily Rude out of her home.

Carrboro issued two press releases last week stating that an investigation into dry cleaning solvent contamination near 408 W. Weaver St. is underway.

The building, which is now occupied by Summerwind Pools and Spas, housed dry cleaning company MEM One-Hour Martinizing during the 1970s.

Rude, who lives directly behind the building, said she first learned of the situation about a month ago when the N.C. Department of Environment and Natural Resources began testing the area.

Rude said department officials installed an air quality tester in her home and found unacceptable levels of contamination.

“It’s a long-term risk exposure, and I don’t want to heighten my risk,” she said. “Who knows how long it’ll take to get the problem fixed?”

Rude and her son are in the process of moving out of the home.

The contamination was first discovered in 2009 when state officials found the dry cleaning solvent Perchloroethylene in a test well at another location.

The owners of the Summerwind building volunteered for testing after the state department’s findings, department spokeswoman Cathy Akroyd wrote in an email.

“This was found to have migrated from the former dry cleaning site at 408 W. Weaver St.,” Akroyd wrote.

Gillings School of Global Public Health professor Ivan Rusyn said some commonly used organic solvents have been linked to several types of diseases and cancer.

Perchloroethylene in particular has been classified by the EPA as likely to cause cancer, he said.

“This particular incident is one of many in the state of North Carolina,” he said. “They have, to my knowledge, a couple of hundred where there is ground water and soil contamination with chlorinated solvents.”

Rusyn, whose lab is studying chlorinated solvents, said the contamination could have occurred after cleaning chemicals were disposed of in an inappropriate container or poured down the drain.

He said human exposure to these chemicals can occur through inhalation or through drinking contaminated water.

Rusyn said responses to exposure of these solvents are classified into two types. Acute responses can be seen soon after exposure and include dizziness or headaches. Long-term responses occur over years or decades and can include kidney tumors and leukemia.

“We’re living in the chemical world,” he said. “If N.C. DENR finds that environmental samples collected at the Carrboro site do exceed safety standards, they have to decide what to do next and what precautions to take.”

Rusyn said further testing will have to occur before the state can determine the severity of the contamination.

“Then people will have to exercise their own judgments as to what is best for them,” he said. “The property owners are going to be in the hardest predicament since this may influence the property values.”
