Finally, differentiated responsibilities are hard to pin down scientifically, since support research on carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries remains limited. Existing studies on this topic remain relatively scarce, mainly when it comes to gathering comprehensive emission data covering marine fisheries as a whole, including fishing activities in the high seas. A 2024 United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) report noted that, because data are so limited, emissions from fishing fleets have been estimated using different methodologies. The report found that bottom-up analyses conducted by the IMO indicated an increasing trend in carbon emissions, whereas top-down approaches suggested a decline. Given this, the report acknowledged that measuring emissions from fishing vessels remains complex, due to many factors involved ( UNCTAD, 2023). For example, research has not yet reached a consensus on emissions from bottom trawling. A 2024 study highlighted growing concerns that seabed disturbances caused by trawling could turn marine sediments into a significant source of carbon dioxide emissions, while noting that these calculations involve substantial uncertainties (). Therefore, without scientific consensus on the baseline scale of emissions, it is hard to accurately assess individual states’ contributions to global carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, their mitigation potential, and their own shares of responsibility. The lack of reliable scientific foundation greatly limits the determination of differentiated responsibilities. Furthermore, the implementation period and compliance standards tied to these responsibilities require continuous scientific assessments and updates. However, there is no dedicated legal mechanism to feed research on high-sea fishery emissions into the formulation, revision, and implementation of mitigation obligations. Then, strengthening scientific knowledge and building science-based assessment mechanisms is essential to making differentiated responsibilities both fair and effective in reducing high-sea fishery carbon emission.

4 Recommendations for applying the principle of CBDR to carbon emission reduction in high seas fisheries

As shown above, applying the CBDR principle to carbon emissions reduction in the high-sea rests on substantial legal and normative foundations. However, the distinctive characteristics of carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries create significant difficulties for their practical implementation. Accordingly, this section proposes recommendations to support the effective application of the CBDR principle to high-sea fishery carbon mitigation.

4.1 Enhancing coordination between the climate change regime and the high seas fisheries governance regime

Applying the CBDR principle to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries cannot succeed through either the climate change regime or the governance regime of high-sea fisheries alone. Instead, an integrated governance approach, built on enhanced coordination and cooperation between the two regimes, is needed.

4.1.1 Division of responsibilities between the climate change regime and the high seas fisheries governance regime

There should be a reasonable division of responsibilities between the climate change regime and the governance regime of high-sea fisheries. The climate-change regime should focus on building political consensus and setting overarching goals, while the high-sea fisheries governance regime should take charge of exploring and implementing specific regulatory approaches. The international community has increasingly come to see the need to treat ocean-related sectors as a distinct category of transboundary emission sources within global climate governance. The United Nations Climate Change Conference has more and more taken up ocean and fisheries issues as part of an “blue climate governance” agenda that goes beyond the traditional framework of territorial emission reduction ( UNFCCC, 2022). However, the roles of the FAO and RFMOs in these discussions have continued to grow, with these institutions gradually taking on functions related to technical coordination, data collection, and capacity building for fishery emissions reduction. Therefore, the prospect of directly extending the existing climate change regime to regulate carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries remains limited. Still, the climate change regime can continue to help build political consensus on high-sea fishery carbon mitigation and strengthen the normative foundation for applying the CBDR principle here. Accordingly, the UNFCCC should mainly handle coordinating overall mitigation goals, mobilizing climate finance, and promoting capacity building, while the FAO and relevant RFMOs should take on the development of specific regulatory measures for carbon reduction in relevant fisheries. Three approaches are considered.

First, under the UNFCCC framework, states could push for developing soft law instruments, such as an initiative for the low-carbon development of high-sea fisheries or a global roadmap for emission reduction in high-sea fisheries. These instruments offer political support and technical guidance for states implementing mitigation measures through RFMOs. Second, the international community should encourage the IPCC to improve scientific research on fishery-related carbon emissions. Building on the Special Report on the Ocean and Cryosphere in a Changing Climate (SROCC), states could push for a dedicated assessment agenda for carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries through the IPCC plenary process. Such an assessment would give an authoritative scientific basis for determining different responsibilities. Third, the international community could explore developing globally used methodologies for carbon accounting in high-sea fisheries, fishing vessel energy-efficiency standards, and guidelines on low-carbon fishing technologies led by the FAO ( Parker and Tyedmers, 2015). RFMOs can also promote regional mechanisms for measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV); vessel carbon intensity management; and green port cooperation (). This approach avoids duplicating institutional efforts among different RFMOs while still accounting for the regional characteristics of high-sea fisheries governance. It should be noted that any carbon mitigation mechanism mainly designed for fisheries should not duplicate the regulatory framework already set out by the IMO. Instead, it should complement and improve the existing architecture of ocean climate governance by addressing the distinctive characteristics of fishery activities and their emission patterns.

4.1.2 Clarifying and expanding the mandate of RFMOs to adopt carbon mitigation measures

The mandate of RFMOs to adopt carbon emission reduction measures in high-sea fisheries should be clarified and improved further. One way to do this through a purposive interpretation of the existing RFMO mandates, thereby gradually widening the legal basis for their involvement in high-sea fishery carbon mitigation. As international institutional law shows, the powers of international organizations are not always confined strictly to matters expressly listed in their constituent instruments. Instead, their mandates can evolve in response to the changing governance needs of the international community. For example, neither the 1944 Convention on International Civil Aviation, which established the ICAO, nor the Convention on the International Maritime Organization, which established the IMO, gave these organizations explicit authority to regulate carbon emissions. Nevertheless, both have gradually developed climate-related regulatory functions through decisions adopted by their respective assemblies (; ). Building on this practice, RFMOs could progressively clarify the connection between carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries and the long-term conservation and sustainable management of fishery resources, using mechanisms such as decisions of contracting party meetings, interpretative documents from scientific committees, and explanatory statements concerning conservation measures. This type of purposive interpretation would let RFMOs set out an initial basis under international law for adopting differentiated carbon mitigation measures without needing formal amendments to existing fishery agreements. In this way, RFMO authority to address climate-related impacts on high-sea fisheries could be improved while opening up institutional space to effectively apply the CBDR principle in allocating carbon emission reduction responsibilities among states engaged in high-sea fisheries.

4.1.3 Adapting the nationally determined contribution mechanism for carbon mitigation in high-seas fisheries

The NDC mechanism established under Article 4 of the Paris Agreement reflects the CBDR principle well. Although the Paris Agreement does not expressly exclude carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries from the scope of NDCs, the mechanism’s voluntary nature gives states little incentives to incorporate these emissions into their national commitments. Additionally, unlike international aviation and maritime transport, the high-sea fisheries sector currently has no globally authoritative body comparable to the ICAO or the IMO. On top of that, overlapping RFMOs memberships make it hard to set a single carbon reduction target across all high-sea fishery areas. Given the regional nature of high-sea fishery governance, it may make more sense for individual RFMOs to develop emission reduction targets suited to their own regional circumstances. Nevertheless, such targets should still be based on commitments voluntarily proposed by members. Accordingly, RFMOs could adopt decisions requiring contracting parties to submit their own carbon emission reduction targets for high-sea fisheries, making clear that such commitments should reflect states’ respective capabilities and national circumstances. This approach would push contracting parties to pay closer attention to carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries while giving RFMOs a foundation for setting regional mitigation goals and applying differentiated emissions reduction measures down the line. By adapting the logic of the NDC mechanism to high-sea fisheries, RFMOs can gradually build a bottom-up mitigation framework that combines flexibility with differentiation, one that fits the evolving interpretation of the CBDR under the Paris Agreement and can accommodate the diversity of states’ fishing capacities, economic conditions, and technological capabilities, while promoting collective action toward low-carbon transformation in high-sea fisheries.

4.2 Incorporating catch volume into the criteria for allocating carbon emission reduction responsibilities in high seas fisheries

High-sea fisheries depend heavily on fossil fuels, so fishing intensity and carbon emissions tend to move together. In general, states that catch more tend to produce higher carbon emissions from high-sea fishing. When adapting the CBDR principle to f high-sea fisheries carbon mitigation, relying solely on the traditional developed-developing country classification has become harder to justify given current realities ( Xu, 2025). Moreover, this classification has faced growing pushback from developed countries, who increasingly question whether a rigid developed country–developing country distinction still makes sense. Compared with purely identity-based classifications, such as the distinction between developed and developing countries, high-sea fishing catch volumes and the corresponding carbon emissions per unit of catch can more directly show states’ actual contributions to carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries. Therefore, these factors offer a more workable basis for reforming and applying the CBDR principle in this field. It is important to note that UNCLOS itself recognizes other categories of differentiation, such as geographically disadvantaged states and landlocked states, which could offer useful reference points for expanding the criteria used to allocate responsibilities. However, because mitigation responsibilities in high-sea fisheries should mainly track the scale of fishing activities, catch volume, as a dynamic indicator that captures changes in states’ high-sea fishing activities, should factor importantly into assessing the size of emission reduction obligations. According to the FAO’s State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2024: Blue Transformation in Action , global capture fisheries are concentrated among few states, which together account for around 25% of catches. These include both traditionally developed fishing nations, such as Japan and the United States, and emerging developing economies, such as China and India (). Therefore, states with high levels of fishing activity should reasonably bear greater emission reduction responsibilities, given their larger contributions to carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries. Nevertheless, incorporating catch volume into the criteria for differentiated responsibilities does not mean abandoning the traditional developed–developing country distinction. Instead, catch volume should add to the existing framework as an additional, activity-based criterion. This multidimensional approach offers a more balanced and realistic basis for applying the CBDR principle to high-sea fisheries carbon mitigation, letting responsibility allocation better reflect differences in historical contributions, current fishing activities, and actual mitigation capacities among states.

First, catch volumes in high-sea fisheries should be split into historical and current catch volumes. Historical catch volumes capture the long-term contributions of members RFMOs to carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries and so should serve as a main basis for allocating mitigation responsibilities ( OECD, 2009). As an marker of historical responsibility for carbon emissions, they are particularly important for building the principle of responsibility for past emissions into the allocation framework. In contrast, current catch volumes reflect present emission scale and future emission trends, and are more flexible in nature. Therefore, they should help adjust mitigation responsibilities and flag priority areas for regulatory oversight, thereby responding to the growing urgency of carbon emissions reduction under worsening climate conditions. On this basis, particular attention should go to carbon emissions per unit catch among different RFMO members, which can indicate each member’s mitigation potential. Considering historical catch-related emissions, current emission levels, and carbon intensity per unit catch together, we can draw a more refined classification of responsibilities within both the developing and developed country groups. Specifically, states can be further sorted into high- and low-responsibility groups based on their emission profiles and mitigation capacities. This differentiated approach moves past the traditional binary distinction between developed and developing countries and allows a more precise allocation of carbon reduction obligations among states. It would also better reflect each member’s actual contribution, current emission scale, and mitigation potential, thereby improving the fairness and effectiveness of applying the CBDR principle to high-sea fisheries carbon emission reduction.

Second, the criteria for allocating carbon emission reduction responsibilities and the specific mitigation measures adopted need to evolve together. Applying the CBDR principle to high-sea fisheries carbon mitigation means adjusting the criteria for identifying responsible states based on the characteristics of high-sea fisheries, as well as differentiating the specific forms and intensity of mitigation obligations. While both developing and developed countries share common responsibilities for reducing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, how these responsibilities are fulfilled should vary according to the states’ historical contributions, current emission levels, and mitigation capacities. Over time, though, these differentiated mitigation approaches should eventually align as states’ capacities and emission profiles change, so as to maximize fairness and ensure the mitigation framework remains effective in the long run. Mainly, states with both low historical and current emissions could primarily take up procedural obligations, such as regularly reporting relevant data on carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries. By contrast, states with high historical and current emissions should take up quantified emission reduction obligations based on their self-determined mitigation targets. A state that has contributed greatly to historical emissions, but currently maintains relatively low emission levels should take up more responsibility for providing financial and technological support to help other states reduce emissions. Conversely, a state with little historical contributions but high current emission levels should prioritize controlling emission growth and improving the carbon intensity of fishing activities. This dynamic and differentiated approach lets CBDR better balance historical responsibility, current emission realities, and future mitigation needs without placing excessive burdens on lower-capacity states or letting major contributors off too lightly.

Third, existing RFMOs should be used to promote catch volume as a criterion for allocating carbon reduction responsibilities. Current RFMO institutional arrangements already provide a suitable foundation for integrating catch volume into the carbon mitigation allocation framework. Most RFMOs have governance structures centered on a decision-making body, such as a commission, supported by subsidiary bodies like scientific, legal, or compliance-related institutions. For example, the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC) includes, besides the Commission itself, subsidiary bodies such as the Scientific Committee, Technical and Compliance Committee, Northern Committee, and Finance and Administration Committee (). These structures offer a practical way of monitoring catch volumes and feeding such data into carbon mitigation governance. Within this framework, different RFMO bodies play complementary roles. First, scientific bodies within RFMOs can take the lead in developing methods for carbon emissions accounting and setting out indicators for carbon emissions per unit of catch. Second, technical and compliance committees can test the level of carbon reduction responsibility individual members should bear, and manage states with different responsibility categories as conditions change. Third, commissions can adopt specific carbon mitigation rules based on catch volume and related emission indicators through legally binding conservation and management measures. Existing RFMOs should set up regular review mechanisms, such as updating responsibility classifications every three to five years, to keep carbon mitigation arrangements responsive to changing fishing patterns, technological developments, and evolving climate conditions. This institutional adaptation allows catch volume to be incorporated into the CBDR framework in a way that is consistent with existing high-sea fisheries governance structures.

4.3 Improving financial mechanisms to support carbon emission reduction in high seas fisheries of developing countries

Developed countries should meet their own development and mitigation obligations, while also providing sustained support in the areas of financing, technology transfer, and capacity building, as required by treaty commitments. Of these three areas, financial support deserves special attention ( Wang et al., 2025). Compared with the other two, financial assistance not only provides the foundation for implementing technological cooperation and capacity enhancement but is also the area where international consensus is most likely to emerge and translate into real actions in the short term.

Both technology transfer and capacity-building run into difficulties during implementation. Existing rules on these two areas under international climate change law and the international law of the sea have commonly fallen short of effective implementation. For example, the Paris Agreement’s provision on financial support mechanisms for technology transfer and capacity building remain fairly general and vague. Similarly, although Part XIV of the UNCLOS established a dedicated framework for developing and transferring marine technology, its practical effectiveness has stayed limited ( Marvasti, 1998). Given this, strengthening financial mechanisms offers a more feasible and immediate path for supporting developing countries in reducing carbon emissions in high-sea fisheries. Adequate and predictable funding gives developing countries what they need to adopt low-carbon fishing technologies, improve vessel efficiency, strengthen emissions monitoring, and take part effectively in international fishery climate governance. Therefore, within the CBDR framework for carbon mitigation in high-sea fisheries, building a targeted and effective financial support mechanism should sit at the core of differentiated responsibilities.

Climate finance sits at the center of global cooperation on climate change. Mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer, and capacity-building efforts under international climate cooperation depend mostly on adequate financial resources ( Yamineva, 2016). Estimates suggest the global shipping sector will need around USD 2.4 trillion to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, and around 500 billion USD by 2030. Financial investment and technology transfer can help developing countries implement effective climate change mitigation measures ( Mayer, 2018). There is currently a big financing gap in global climate action. According to the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), annual investment in renewable energy needs to rise to approximately USD 800 billion to keep the global temperature rise below 2 °C under the Paris Agreement ( IRENA, 2020). Similarly, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) estimates that global investment of around USD 8.1 trillion is needed by 2050 to effectively address climate-related crises ( UNEP, 2021). The Paris Agreement prioritizes the responsibility of developed countries to provide climate finance. Article 9 explicitly requires developed-country parties to continue to keep leading in providing financial resources. During the 2009 Copenhagen Climate Conference, developed countries pledged to mobilize USD 100 billion annually in climate finance for developing countries by 2020 ( OECD, 2026). Later, under the Paris Agreement adopted in 2015, developed countries agreed to mobilize at least USD 100 billion per year in new climate finance after 2025 to support developing countries in addressing climate change ( UNFCCC, 2024). When it comes to carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries, financial support could help developing countries to implement effective mitigation measures, including improving fishing vessel efficiency, adopting low-carbon technologies, and strengthening emissions monitoring capabilities. Moreover, setting up a financial mechanism specifically for supporting developing countries in reducing carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries would allow differentiated responsibilities to be realized without clashing with the principle of nondiscrimination traditionally applied in high-sea fisheries governance. It would also make sure the implementation of the CBDR does not undermine the freedom of fishing in the high seas, which rests fundamentally on the principle of sovereign equality among states. As the institutional and scientific understanding of carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries keeps developing, differentiated responsibilities may appear through a broader range of mitigation measures. For now, though, financial support provides a relatively feasible and legally compatible approach for operationalizing the CBDR principle in this field, since it reconciles the need for differentiated obligations with the fundamental principles of high-sea fisheries governance.

First, a dedicated financial mechanism for carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries should be established under the framework of the 1995 Fish Stocks Agreement. Part VII of the Agreement directly addresses the “requirements of developing states” and sets up a framework for international cooperation to support their participation in the conservation and management of straddling and highly migratory fish stocks. Article 25 states that forms of cooperation with developing states can take the form of financial assistance, help with human resource development, and technology transfer through joint venture arrangements, as well as advisory and consultancy services. Of these, financial assistance stands out as an important means of supporting developing states. Furthermore, Article 26 of the Agreement requires the establishment of special assistance mechanisms to support developing states in implementing agreements. Paragraph 1 of Article 26 states that states should cooperate to establish special funds to assist developing states in implementing the Agreement, including helping them cover the costs of dispute settlement procedures they may be involved in. Based on Part VII of the 1995 Fish Stocks Agreement, the United Nations General Assembly established an assistance fund on November 24, 2003, to assist developing states Parties in implementing the Agreement. This fund was jointly administered by the FAO and the Division for Ocean Affairs and Law of the Sea (DOALOS) (). However, due to insufficient funding, the assistance fund eventually exhausted its available resources and ceased operations (). Even so, developing states can still rely on the framework established under Part VII of the Fish Stocks Agreement to establish a dedicated financial mechanism for carbon emissions reduction in high-sea fisheries. Such a mechanism could require developed states to provide enhanced financial support to developing states, mainly to speed up the replacement and upgrade of outdated fishing vessels, promote the development of environmentally friendly and energy-efficient fishing vessels and gear, and support the research and deployment of low-carbon fishing technologies. By building upon the cooperative obligations already recognized under the Fish Stocks Agreement, such a financial mechanism would provide an existing legal path for operationalizing the CBDR principle in high-sea fisheries. It would also help avoid placing disproportionate mitigation burdens on developing states while boosting their capacity to participate effectively in global efforts to reduce emissions from fishing activities in the high seas.

Second, dedicated mechanisms for financing carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries should be developed within the existing green climate finance frameworks. Right now, both the Green Climate Fund (GCF) and Global Environment Facility (GEF) operate based on NDCs, which highlight that emission reductions should be attributable to emission activities occurring within a specific state’s territorial jurisdiction. However, given the distinctive characteristics of high-sea fisheries, it is hard to apply existing climate finance mechanisms directly to mitigation projects in this sector. Therefore, it is necessary to establish a specialized financial support mechanism for high-sea fishery carbon mitigation within the broader framework of international climate finance. Specifically, priority should go to establishing a dedicated high-sea fishery emission reduction window under the GCF framework. Such mechanism should move beyond the existing project eligibility model centered on territorial emissions and let emission reductions from high-sea fisheries be accounted for based on flag states. This approach addresses the institutional obstacles under the current GCF framework, under which emission reductions from high-sea activities are difficult to attribute to a specific state’s territorial emission inventory. This mechanism should fully reflect the principles of CBDR in terms of funding sources. To operationalize this financing mechanism, developed countries should make binding baseline financial contributions. Such an obligation is justified by their long-standing advantages in distant-water fishing technologies, capital investment, and seafood consumption, as well as their historical contribution to carbon emissions associated with global marine resource exploitation. Building upon this foundational financial commitment, the international community could explore the establishment of an international carbon levy or fee for high-emission distant-water fishing activities, with the revenue earmarked for a dedicated high-sea fisheries carbon mitigation fund. In parallel, international organizations, multinational enterprises, and private capital could be encouraged to participate through voluntary contributions, thereby gradually establishing a diversified financing structure. Regarding fund allocation, priority should be given to supporting developing countries. Key areas of support should include energy-efficiency upgrades for aging distant-water fishing vessels, the replacement of low-carbon fishing equipment, pilot projects involving alternative fuels, and the development of green port infrastructure. In particular, demonstration projects using low-carbon technologies such as liquefied natural gas (LNG) and ammonia-based fuels should be actively promoted in the high-sea fisheries sector. In addition, the development of measurement, reporting, and verification (MRV) capacity should be identified as a priority area for financial support. Assistance should be provided to developing countries to set up systems for monitoring, reporting, and verifying carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, thereby enhancing their ability to participate effectively in the formulation and implementation of international rules on carbon reduction in high-sea fisheries. Through such a dedicated financial mechanism, the CBDR principle can be operationalized in a manner that combines differentiated responsibilities with enhanced capacity-building, ensuring that developing countries participate equitably in the global transition toward low-carbon fisheries.

5 Conclusion

This study examined how the CBDR principle applies to carbon emission reduction in high-sea fisheries, analyzed the practical challenges of putting it into practice, and proposed recommendations for addressing them. As pressure mounts to cut carbon emissions from high-sea fisheries, whether states can allocate mitigation responsibilities under the CBDR principle is a key prerequisite for any collective international measures. The analysis shows that, in high-sea fisheries, states share common responsibilities for carbon emissions reduction but also hold differentiated responsibilities rooted in differences in historical emissions, mitigation capacities, and relevant legal obligations. On this basis, this study identified several major challenges in applying the CBDR principle to carbon mitigation in high-sea fisheries: whether the principle should be carried out through the climate change regime or the high-sea fisheries governance regime, what criteria should determine which states bear mitigation obligations, and what forms of differentiated responsibilities should be adopted. Resolving these issues is essential to putting the CBDR principle to effective use in high-sea fisheries carbon emission reduction. To address these challenges, this study proposes several measures, including promoting functional cooperation and coordination between the climate change regime and the high-sea fisheries governance regime, clarifying and reinforcing RFMO’s authority to adopt carbon mitigation measures, adapting the NDC mechanism for use in high-sea fisheries, factoring catch volume into the criteria for allocating carbon reduction responsibilities, setting up a dedicated financial mechanism for high-sea fisheries carbon mitigation under the framework of the Fish Stocks Agreement, and promoting the development of specialized financing mechanisms for high-sea fisheries emission reduction within existing green climate finance frameworks. These measures together can help operationalize the CBDR principle in high-sea fishery carbon emissions governance, laying a more equitable and effective legal foundation for international cooperation and collective action toward a low-carbon transformation in global fisheries.

This study had certain limitations that point to useful directions for future research. First, the analysis mainly takes a legal and institutional approach and does not quantitatively assess how different fishing activities and actors contribute to GHG emissions. Future research should develop better methodologies for measuring emissions from high-sea fisheries and further examine how indicators, such as fuel consumption, fishing effort, catch volume, and historical emissions, could help allocate mitigation responsibilities. Second, although this study examines the relationship between climate governance and fisheries governance frameworks, more empirical work is needed to compare how different RFMOs build differentiated mitigation obligations into their regulatory practices. Such research could offer valuable insights into how feasible and practical it truly is to implement the CBDR principle across the many different high-sea fishery governance arrangements. This study highlights the broader challenges international law faces in regulating emissions from global activities. Existing climate governance still relies heavily on territorial and state-centered approaches, whereas activities beyond national jurisdiction involve complex networks of actors, transboundary emission sources, and overlapping institutional arrangements. Therefore, future research should explore more integrated governance models that connect climate law, the law of the sea, and fisheries governance, and should also look at how principles of equity can be turned into workable mechanisms for allocating carbon emission reduction responsibilities in the global commons. This work could help build a more adaptive and inclusive international legal framework, one that is capable of addressing the unique governance challenges posed by carbon emissions from high-sea activities.

text:
Article Insights

Highlights

Three U.S. House of Representatives hearings held in July 2026 – one before the Committee on Education and the Workforce and two before the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform's Task Force on Defending Constitutional Rights and Exposing Institutional Abuses – show congressional scrutiny of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs expanding beyond admissions into curricula, faculty policy, campus programming and accreditation.

A single theme ran through all three hearings: members suggesting that institutions had renamed DEI programs rather than dismantled them and noting that a change in office names, course titles and website copy was not evidence of compliance.

The signaling of additional congressional activity is converging with executive branch enforcement, including U.S. Department of Justice Title VI investigations, False Claims Act exposure under the Civil Rights Fraud Initiative and new federal accreditation regulations. Public materials, internal documents and prior compliance certifications will likely be examined together.

As institutions wrestle with ongoing scrutiny from the administration and congressional Republicans, Democratic officials have weighed in as well, seeking information on how institutions have responded to the current administration, including what concessions have been made.

The U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Education and the Workforce held a hearing on July 14, 2026, titled “Training Activists, Not Physicians: The Impact of DEI on Medical Schools,” with testimony from leaders of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) David Geffen School of Medicine, University of California, San Francisco and University of Illinois College of Medicine, along with the president of the National Medical Association. The committee opened investigations into the three medical schools in 2025.

Republican members focused on course content, reading specific phrases and course titles into the record and asking whether those subjects were still taught. Witnesses testified that the diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)-focused courses at issue had been discontinued before any congressional inquiry, that the institutions had limited required instruction to their own faculty and that classroom time had been restricted to relevant course content. Members also pressed on U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) Civil Rights Division findings regarding the use of race in UCLA medical school admissions, on compliance with executive orders addressing federally funded DEI programs and institutional practices relating to care for transgender minors. Witnesses declined to address matters subject to ongoing litigation.

Notably, members treated curricular changes made before the investigation as a reason to ask what prompted them, and they cited institutional websites that still referenced diversity and inclusion as evidence that reforms were incomplete. Following the hearing, the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights opened admissions discrimination investigations into five additional medical schools.

"Combating DEI in American Institutions"

The Oversight Task Force hearing of the same title focused on what members and witnesses described as the persistence of DEI functions under new names. Witnesses testified that DEI personnel frequently remain in place under relabeled offices and pointed to identity-based commencement events as an example of programming that continues in substance. Testimony also urged federal enforcers to shift emphasis from disparate impact theories toward cases alleging intentional discrimination.

Law School Accreditation and the ABA

The Task Force's hearing on "The Future of DEI in Law School Accreditation and the Legal Profession" centered on the American Bar Association (ABA) and its role as the sole federally recognized accreditor of law schools. Republican members criticized ABA Accreditation Standard 206, which requires law schools to demonstrate a commitment to diversity and inclusion, and Standard 303(c), which requires coursework on bias, cross-cultural competency and racism. Witnesses urged Congress and the Education Department to recognize additional law school accreditors and bar recognition of any accreditor that imposes DEI requirements. The ABA's president testified the organization is nonpartisan and that the Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar operates independently of the broader association. Democratic members argued that the council, not the ABA president, was the appropriate witness.

The ABA has already moved on both standards. Enforcement of Standard 206 has been suspended since February 2025, the suspension has been extended into 2027, and the council voted in May 2026 to repeal it. That repeal is not final. The ABA's House of Delegates declined to concur on August 4, 2026, and the council is expected to take the standard up again later this month. Standard 303(c) remains under review. Committee members nevertheless expressed skepticism that these steps reflect a durable change in position.

The Converging Enforcement Environment

The hearings are one component of a broader landscape institutions are evaluating as a whole.

Justice Department Civil Rights Enforcement: The DOJ Civil Rights Division has opened more than 100 investigations into university admissions practices and issued findings against several medical schools. Those include UCLA's David Geffen School of Medicine, which was represented at the July hearing. In June 2026, the Division also announced an additional 15 medical school investigations and opened a Title VI investigation into university DEI practices. A June 16, 2026, interagency agreement between the Education Department and DOJ gives DOJ a substantially larger role in investigating and resolving civil rights complaints against educational institutions – a shift that brings litigation-style tools, including formal data demands and witness interviews, to matters historically handled through administrative processes at the Education Department's Office for Civil Rights. Most recently, in August, DOJ issued findings against a law school alleging that its admissions practices continued to consider race following the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, 600 U.S. 181 (2023), including through facially neutral admissions criteria that DOJ contends operated as proxies for race.

False Claims Act (FCA) Exposure: DOJ's Civil Rights Fraud Initiative, established in May 2025, uses the FCA against federal funding recipients that certify compliance with civil rights laws while allegedly maintaining discriminatory programs. The initiative reaches any recipient of federal funds, which places universities and academic medical centers within its scope alongside contractors. The first public resolution came in April 2026 when a federal contractor agreed to pay $17 million to resolve allegations tied to its DEI programs. Institutions that certified civil rights compliance when accepting federal grants or contracts should expect those certifications, and the records behind them, to be examined against actual practice.

Accreditation Rulemaking: The Education Department's Accreditation, Innovation and Modernization negotiated rulemaking committee reached consensus in May 2026 on proposed amendments to 34 C.F.R. Parts 600, 602 and 668. The draft would ease recognition of new accreditors, require greater separation between accrediting agencies and affiliated trade associations, add civil rights and viewpoint diversity requirements and refocus review on student outcomes. The proposed rule has moved into the final stages of executive branch review ahead of publication in the Federal Register. Once published, the Education Department will open a public comment period, likely 30 days, before issuing a final rule. If the Department issues a final rule by November 1, 2026, it will take effect July 1, 2027.

State-Level Fragmentation in Legal Education: Several states are reconsidering exclusive reliance on ABA accreditation for bar eligibility. The Alabama Supreme Court has amended its bar admission rule to allow graduates of non-ABA-accredited law schools to sit for the exam, and similar measures are under discussion elsewhere. Law schools face the prospect of divergent state requirements and questions about bar exam portability for their graduates.

The Education Department's "National Call to Action": On August 3, 2026, U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon issued an open letter to all university presidents and governing boards asking each institution to publish, by the end of 2026, a public statement addressing seven questions on admissions transparency, free speech, intellectual pluralism, affordability, academic rigor, research security and national service. Unlike the October 2025 compact, which was offered to a limited group of institutions before being extended more broadly, the letter imposes no mandate, conditions no funding and specifies no consequence for declining. Time will tell whether any institutions respond to the request.

Potential Risk

Institutions find themselves in a challenging position: complying with demands from the Trump Administration that may then open them to questions and actions from Democratic policymakers about what concessions have been made. For example, when the administration circulated its 2025 compact, California's governor threatened to withhold state funds from any signatory, Virginia Senate Democratic leadership warned a state university of budget consequences, and Pennsylvania legislators moved to bar state-funded institutions from participating. Senate Democrats led by Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) have separately pressed the Education Department over accreditor recognition – the mechanism at issue in the law school hearing – and 19 state attorneys general and the attorney general for the District of Columbia sued in June 2026 over the federal contractor DEI executive order.

It's worth noting that positions taken now by institutions of higher education – whether in response to the Education Department's call to action, commitments made to resolve federal investigations and/or program changes – will be available to a differently constituted Congress in January 2027, as well as to state officials and private litigants in the meantime.

What Institutions Should Consider Now

Congressional investigations create exposure that differs from litigation or agency enforcement – namely, legal risk, reputational harm, funder scrutiny and political pressure. As such, institutions with potential exposure may want to consider the following steps:

Audit Public-Facing Materials. Websites, course catalogs, office names, scholarship criteria, event descriptions and admissions materials are the primary source documents for congressional staff. Inconsistency between what an institution says publicly and what it has certified to federal agencies is itself an investigative predicate.

Assess Substance, Not Just Labels. Renaming an office or removing a webpage does not resolve the underlying question of whether decisions turn on protected characteristics. Review admissions, hiring, scholarship and programming criteria against the standards the government is applying and document the basis for changes already made.

Reconcile Certifications with Practice. Identify federal grants and contracts carrying civil rights certifications and confirm that the underlying facts support them.

Prepare for Parallel Proceedings. Congressional inquiries frequently run alongside DOJ, the Education Department and state attorney general matters. Positions taken in one forum will be used in the others, and congressional testimony is not privileged.

Treat Any Response to the Education Department's Call to Action as a Durable Public Commitment. Participation is voluntary, and the decision whether and how to respond should be made with counsel, governance and communications input. Whatever is published should be accurate today and defensible in two years.

Establish Document Retention and Response Protocols Before a Request Arrives. Also, coordinate legal, compliance, government relations and communications functions in advance.

text:
The story so far:

The Assam government recently announced plans to approach the Centre to shrink the Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ), a buffer zone around protected areas, to a minimum of 1 km instead of the default 10 km. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma’s argument that an ESZ of more than 1 km around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve would affect civic and urban growth in surrounding towns has stoked controversy and raised questions about the government’s seriousness about conserving natural assets.

Also read | Assam CM defends move to reduce Kaziranga Eco-Sensitive Zone to 1 km from the default 10 km

What is an ESZ?

Also known as an Ecologically Fragile Area, an ESZ is a buffer zone or a wide demarcated strip around national parks and wildlife sanctuaries protected by law to stop heavy human damage, lower human-animal conflicts, and improve conservation of natural assets.

The National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) adopted a resolution in 2002 to declare such buffer zones around protected areas under the Environment (Protection) Act of 1986. As part of the National Wildlife Action Plan (2002-2016), the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) instructed the State governments in 2011 to submit site-specific proposals for ESZs, with a general guideline that a buffer zone should be up to 10 km from the periphery of a protected area. The guidelines allowed an ESZ to exceed the 10-km limit to include larger ecologically important sensitive corridors, connectivity patches, and vital landscape linkages.

Why are ESZs important?

According to the NBWL, an ESZ is envisaged as a shock absorber to minimise the impact of certain human activities on the fragile ecosystem of the protected areas. In other words, it is considered a transition zone between high-protection areas and low-protection areas, without affecting the daily activities of people living in the vicinity. Such activities have three categories—prohibited, regulated and permitted.

The prohibited activities include commercial mining, sawmills, industries causing air, water, soil and noise pollution, hydroelectric projects, discharge of effluents or solid waste and certain tourism events. Among the regulated activities are felling of trees, establishment of hotels and resorts, commercial use of natural water, erection of electric cables, widening of roads and drastic change of agricultural system with the use of heavy technology, pesticides, etc. The permitted activities include ongoing eco-friendly agricultural or horticultural practices, rainwater harvesting, the use of renewable energy sources and adoption of green technology. All these are intended to minimise the impact of urbanisation and other developmental activities on the flora and fauna in the protected areas.

Can the extent of an ESZ be reduced?

According to the rules, the default 10 km ESZ extent remains in force for protected areas unless a State government submits or receives a final, site-specific notification approved by the MoEFCC.

Assam has eight national parks, more than 20 existing and proposed wildlife sanctuaries, and other protected areas with ESZ varying by site. While a few have site-specific draft or final notifications, the rhino-centric Kaziranga operates under the default rule pending final tailored notifications.

The Chief Minister cited the case of Deepor Beel, a Ramsar Site on the south-western edge of Guwahati, to argue that Bokakhat, Kaliabor and other surrounding towns warrant a 1-km ESZ for Kaziranga.

The MoEFCC’s July 2025 draft notification for Deepor Beel notes the “immense biotic pressure” on the wetland due to expanding human settlements, industrial units, discharge of city waste and industrial effluents, and a railway track along its southern boundary. It prescribes an extent of 25.294 metres to 5 km around the Deepor Beel Bird Sanctuary (covering 4.1 sq. km within a wetland that extends up to 40 sq. km in the summer and reduces to about 10 sq. km in winter), encompassing an ESZ of 38.84 sq. km.

The Chief Minister also referred to a Supreme Court order to announce plans to approach the Centre for a baseline ESZ buffer of 1 to 3 km around Kaziranga. Based on objections from some States, specifically Kerala, which wanted the ESZ around Wayanad Wildlife Sanctuary reduced from 118.59 sq. km down to 88.21 sq. km, the Supreme Court modified its June 2022 order that mandated a uniform 1-km ESZ around all protected forests.

In April 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that a one-size-fits-all ESZ is not feasible, exempting areas with existing draft or final notifications and allowing basic local infrastructure, while maintaining a strict ban on commercial mining near sanctuaries.

How will a reduced ESZ impact Kaziranga?

The Chief Minister’s announcement has elicited strong reactions.

Jadab Payeng, a grassroots environmental activist based east of Kaziranga, urged the government to stick to 10 km as the ESZ for the UNESCO World Heritage Site given the frequent human-animal conflicts. He said Kaziranga’s reputation as one of the best protected national parks in the world would suffer otherwise.

Assam Congress president Gaurav Gogoi and environmental groups questioned the proposal against wider ecological protection, warning that a shrinking buffer zone for the 1,302 sq. km Kaziranga Tiger Reserve could harm animal migration routes during annual floods.

The worry is more about the southern boundary of the rhino domain blending into the hills of Karbi Anglong district across National Highway-715 (formerly NH-27), where animals take refuge when the core area of the national park is flooded. Stone quarrying and riverbed mining in these hills—a Karbi Anglong-based activist recently flagged large-scale sand extraction and use of heavy machinery in the Deihori River—close to the park have been threatening vital wildlife corridors and local hydrology.

There are also allegations against influential political leaders, their family members and business houses having established or pursuing hotels and resorts within the proposed ESZ. Local farmers have been opposing one such luxury hotel project for which Pranab Doley, a land rights activist, has been detained under the National Security Act.

Erthos solar modules are mounted directly on the earth without structural steel, streamlining development and enabling the solar energy system to generate electricity at a lower cost

ForeFront Power, a leading developer and asset manager of commercial and industrial-scale renewable energy solutions, on Thursday announced that it has achieved commercial operation of its first Erthos solar energy system at the City of Fresno’s Northeast Surface Water Treatment Plant.

Erthos distills the complexity of solar energy systems into a modular, repeatable design. Unlike traditional ground-mounted solar energy systems supported by structural steel, Erthos’ Earth Mount Solar system places modules directly on the earth, which allows solar project developers to eliminate all the costs required to procure and install structural steel. Leveraging Erthos technology, ForeFront Power was able to reduce its total cost to develop its solar energy system and pass those savings to the City of Fresno in the form of lower electricity rates.

ForeFront Power approached Erthos in 2023 when a combination of inflation and supply shocks caused the price of labor and materials to spike. The ForeFront Power team realized that the cost of a traditional ground-mounted system at this site would be significantly higher. This in turn would increase the cost of the electricity that ForeFront Power would sell back to the City of Fresno through a Power Purchase Agreement. Under the terms of the Agreement, ForeFront Power owns the system and charges the City a fixed, lower rate for electricity than the utility for 20 years.

“After conducting our due diligence and vetting Erthos technology, we discovered that the Northeast Surface Water Treatment Plant was an optimal site for an Erthos application,” said Erinne Davis, senior project manager at ForeFront Power. “Erthos helped us avoid significant, expensive civil upgrades, as well as the cost of steel for racking and the labor to install that racking. Realizing these savings on the installation is what enabled the project at this site to move forward.”

The Erthos Earth Mount Solar system is part of a sprawling solar energy and smart battery storage portfolio that ForeFront Power developed for the City of Fresno’s Department of Public Utilities (DPU) at three sites: the Northeast Surface Water Treatment Facility, the Southeast Surface Water Treatment Facility, and the Fresno-Clovis Regional Wastewater Reclamation Facility. At a combined 27 MW-DC in size, the DPU projects are expected to save over $122 million in ratepayer dollars by 2045.

Since the system entered commercial operation in late March 2026, the system has consistently outperformed expectations, operating at an average of 101% of expected energy production and has already delivered 862 MWh of energy to the City. ForeFront Power and Erthos continue to work closely together to optimize system performance. Both organizations are encouraged by the project’s early results and outlook for continued strong performance in the years ahead.

How Erthos Enables a Lower Cost Per Watt for Solar Electricity

In addition to avoiding material and labor costs from structural steel, ForeFront Power was able to achieve a higher generating capacity per acre thanks to the unique architecture of Erthos systems. With no row spacing, Erthos offers the highest energy density of any solar architecture in the industry. Another unique feature of Erthos Earth Mount Solar system is that, although the solar modules are mounted flat on the earth, they can follow contours up to 15% slope, meaning they were adaptable to the natural topography of the Fresno site.

ForeFront Power and Erthos have entered into an Energy Services Agreement in which Erthos will maintain the solar energy system, including regular cleanings of the solar array by their proprietary ErthBot PV array cleaner, a dry nylon brush autonomous cleaning robot. Each ErthBot is designed to clean over 3.5 MW-DC of solar PV array, making it the most cost-effective method for cleaning large-scale PV arrays in the industry.

Custom-designed for use on an Earth Mount Solar array, the ErthBot cleaner is deployed nightly as needed and returns to its charging dock after each use, ready to be deployed again the following evening. Erthos handles the operations and maintenance of the ErthBot as part of its Energy Services Agreement with ForeFront Power.

“The Fresno project demonstrates how Erthos Earth Mount Solar can unlock projects that might otherwise be constrained by conventional construction costs,” said Jim Tyler, CEO of Erthos. “Working with ForeFront Power, we delivered a high-density solar system designed for strong long-term performance, efficient maintenance, and lower-cost energy for the City of Fresno.”

About ForeFront Power

ForeFront Power is a leading provider of energy solutions and advisory services. This includes commercial and industrial-scale (C&I) solar energy and battery storage projects in the U.S. and Mexico, as well as fleet electrification and asset management services. With over 15 years of experience, the ForeFront Power team has developed more than 1,900 behind-the-meter and community solar projects, totaling more than 1.6 gigawatt-DC of renewable electricity. In addition to project development and asset management, ForeFront Power provides strategic advisory services that help organizations navigate complex energy decisions—from sustainability and procurement planning to renewable project implementation. The company serves a wide array of business, government, education, healthcare, and community solar customers from its San Francisco headquarters and through teams based in New York, Mexico City, and across the U.S. For additional information, please visit www.forefrontpower.com.

A network of hundreds of geothermal wells, each one plunging hundreds of feet underground, is taking shape at Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport/Adams Field in Little Rock as part of an overhaul of the complex's utility systems.

Work on the well field started in August 2025. Drilling and grouting of the wells themselves finished in May, according to David Finnie, the director of infrastructure development for the airport.

Each well descends 500 feet below the surface. Temperatures that deep underground remain fairly constant year-round, even as the seasons change and atmospheric temperatures rise and fall.

By pumping water or other fluid through geothermal wells, those stable temperatures can be harnessed for heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems.

Crews at the airport are now linking the wells in groups of around 25 wells known as circuits, which are then each tied to a vault that routes hot and cold water flowing through the system, Finnie said in an interview.

"It's kind of a complex little system," he said.

When completed, water will be circulated through the system in a closed loop, allowing for efficient heating and cooling of the airport terminal.

Officials expect the project will eliminate all natural gas usage at the airport, Finnie said, with the exception of cooking needs at restaurants in the concourse.

The well field is located to the east of the airport terminal and north of an employee parking lot, with some wells located on the east side of the lot.

Officials eventually plan to construct a new parking lot on top of the well field, Finnie said. He estimated that the well field consists of about six acres, or around one-third of the size of the future parking lot.

Officials are pursuing the geothermal project in conjunction with an effort to construct a new central utility plant. Rerouting the airport's utility infrastructure inside the new plant will allow crews to renovate the terminal to add a new arrivals hall and post-security common area over the coming years.

Finnie estimated construction of the central utility plant will conclude in the summer of 2027. Once it is complete, the geothermal well field will go online, he said.

In 2024, the airport was awarded $7.5 million from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to help pay for the geothermal well field project. The funding was part of a nearly $100 million award to a coalition of Arkansas regional planning organizations through the Climate Pollution Reduction Grants program, created through the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022. Metroplan, the metropolitan planning organization for Central Arkansas, led the coalition.

The total cost of the airport geothermal project will be close to $39 million, with additional support from a Federal Aviation Administration low-emissions grant program as well as tax credits, according to Finnie.

text:
Global sales of EVs and plug-in hybrids rose in July, even as North America saw a sharp drop after federal incentives expired, suggesting the shift to cleaner cars is still underway — just not at the same pace everywhere.

Here's what to know

According to The Drive, global EV and plug-in hybrid sales in July were 9% higher than in July 2025.

In contrast, North American EV sales fell 27% year over year after federal incentives expired.

July also broke a six-month stretch of falling U.S. EV prices. Prices rose 1.2% from June 2026 and 1.6% from July 2025.

The rebound in pricing tracked with a pullback in incentive spending by automakers.

The end of federal incentives and fewer discounts from manufacturers can make an already costly purchase even less attainable.

More background

Global momentum can continue even as one region slows down, particularly when public policy, charging access, and vehicle pricing vary from country to country.

For many households, the biggest obstacle is still the upfront cost. While EVs can reduce spending over time through lower fuel and maintenance expenses, a higher sticker price can still keep many buyers from making the switch.

If incentives disappear just as automaker discounts shrink, the monthly payment can become much harder to justify.

The slowdown is also reaching beyond dealership lots. A lack of demand left General Motors' and LG's Ohio battery plant idle for seven months, though production is expected to restart in August 2026.

The pause affects the broader supply chain, including battery manufacturing and jobs tied to EV production.

At the same time, rising global sales show that buyers and automakers in other parts of the world are still moving ahead with electrification, even as North America's market becomes less supportive.

What's being done?

Automakers still have several options to help keep EV adoption moving after federal incentives end.

One of the biggest is pricing. Companies can bring back or expand their own discounts, financing offers, or lease deals to make EVs more affordable for buyers.

Another is product strategy, including a stronger focus on smaller and lower-cost EVs that appeal to mainstream drivers rather than just premium customers.

Restarting the Ohio battery plant could also help stabilize supply if demand improves. Keeping domestic battery production running also supports manufacturing jobs and efforts to build lower-cost EVs closer to where they are sold.

July's numbers do not suggest the EV transition has come to a halt. They do, however, show that cost support remains a major factor in whether cleaner cars are a realistic choice for everyday drivers.

More than 70 years of gas vehicle production at Ford's Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky are giving way to a fully electric future.

Ford says the site, one of its longtime manufacturing hubs, is in the middle of a $2 billion overhaul to prepare for the Fathom EV truck.

Here's what to know

On Aug. 13, Ford told InsideEVs that the Louisville Assembly Plant's retooling for Fathom production had been completed, though a later update from Ford confirmed that the conversion was still underway.

Getting the factory ready for EV production meant removing 25,000 tons of older equipment, which was hauled away in more than 2,600 truckloads for recycling. Ford also poured concrete across more than 230,000 square feet of floor space. Before that shift, the plant had been building gas-powered models including the Ford Escape and Lincoln Corsair.

Ford said the redesigned factory will use a new "assembly tree" process rather than relying solely on a traditional moving assembly line. Under that setup, large sections of the vehicle are assembled separately and connected late in the process, with one section holding the structural battery along with the seats, consoles, and carpeting, InsideEVs reported.

The company expects the new process to cut net assembly time by 15%, making jobs easier on workers' bodies and helping catch software issues earlier in production.

More background

Affordable EV production has become one of the biggest questions in the auto industry. Ford has said the Fathom will start at around $30,000, meaning the success of this plant could help determine whether the company can scale up a lower-cost electric pickup.

More EV options can mean more opportunities to save money over time. Electric vehicles typically cost less to fuel than gas-powered cars and usually require less routine maintenance because they do not need oil changes and have fewer moving parts that wear out.

Many drivers are looking into buying an electric vehicle, especially as automakers work to bring prices down. A factory designed for faster, more efficient EV assembly could help support that trend.

Retiring older gas-only production equipment and shifting toward battery-powered models can help reduce tailpipe pollution, especially if EV adoption continues to grow.

What's being done?

Ford's new production strategy is focused on both manufacturing speed and worker comfort. Instead of requiring workers to reach into cramped cabins to install parts late in the process, the company says key components can be added earlier, when the vehicle sections are still easier to access.

Bryce Currie, Ford chief manufacturing officer, said in a statement, "We listened to all the things operators don't like." Ford also says software modules can now be updated and tested before they are installed in the vehicle, reducing the chance that a problem will slow down final assembly.

For drivers thinking about making the switch, charging costs are also part of the equation. Charging an EV at home can cost less than using public chargers, but basic Level 1 charging tends to be slow. Qmerit provides installation estimates for faster Level 2 home charger installations.
